Developing CS NLP models is hindered by the scarcity and quality of Arabic-English CS data, whereas data augmentation methods utilizing modern language models have the potential to mitigate this limitation. We examined the effectiveness of utilizing BERT-based models for CS information augmentation in Arabic-English. Our study involved an in-depth examination of the impact of lexical substitutions on the authenticity and relevance of augmented data, and found that incorporating both CS and MS lexical substitutions significantly enhances the quality of augmented data. We discovered that incorporating MS lexical substitutions almost doubles the CS lexical substitution rate without compromising the augmented text's Arabic-English CS consistency. When used separately, the CS lexical substitution task performs better in terms of augmented text consistency, whereas the MS lexical substitution task performs better in terms of augmented text quality and fluency. We utilized BERTscore as the primary evaluation metric and annotator agreements were found to be consistent across different augmentation methods. We open-source our project on GitHub. Our research indicates that RACE is an suitable model architecture for CS information augmentation in Arabic-English. We also identified through human assessment that the generated text quality is affected by the level of proficiency in both Arabic and English languages. We discovered that more fluent text is generated when the source language is English. We propose that the generated text should be post-edited by native speakers to ensure linguistic accuracy and authenticity. Our study sets the groundwork for an investigation on the impact of lexical substitutions on the CSNLP task of generating summary snippets. We obtained human judgments on the augmented snippets quality and conducted an A/B testing study to compare the effectiveness of different CS information augmentation methods in improving model performance in the snippet generation task. The study demonstrated that using MS lexical substitutions leads to higher MRR and recall values and improved f1 scores compared to the CS lexical substitution alone. It appears that a certain degree of CS lexical substitution variability is necessary for enhanced information augmentation. We observed that models performing well on augmented data tend to generalize poorly to real CS text. We hope our research sparks future investigation into the impact of lexical substitutions on the CSNLP task of generating summary snippets. Such a study may lead to a more profound understanding of the relationship between CS lexical variability and augmented data quality, ultimately yielding improved performance in the snippet generation task. We found that a key aspect of CS information augmentation is the consistency between the CS used in the source and target text. Therefore, it would be interesting to explore the impact of lexical substitutions on the CSNLP task of machine translation, a study which may culminate in enhanced translation accuracy.

Although hexahedral meshes offer superior analytical properties compared to other discretization methods, their full potential is hindered by the high computational cost associated with the necessary finite element calculations. Nonetheless, the development of efficient numerical algorithms has ultimately replaced theoretical limitations, enabling numerical solutions to engineering problems previously thought intractable by the hexahedral method. This work begins with a historical perspective on the development of hexahedral mesh methods, before presenting a selection of efficient numerical algorithms optimized to take full advantage of the inherent properties inherent in hexahedral meshes, resulting in superior solution efficiency. Notably, many of these algorithms integrate well with the recursive mesh trigonometry, a fundamental unit of space that facilitates innovative problem modeling. These example problems serve as a benchmark to the hexahedral method, similar to those previously carried out for nodal methods in Ref. [hex-2005b]. This work is intended as an offering to the scientific community, providing a comprehensive hexahedral method library consisting of efficient numerical algorithms, adaptable geometry models, and an extensive collection of successful application examples. Human-robot interaction could be improved by models of social interaction that incorporate motivation, as current systems often lack the mental underlying state driving their responses, leaving them appearing mechanical and overly critical. This research aims to develop a more nuanced approach by incorporating an internal state of motivation in robots. A novel method of incentive design is proposed, which assesses and adjusts the level of motivation based on the behavior of human collaborators. A simulation study demonstrates that our approach can enhance transfer learning in robots and improves their overall performance. A real-world robotic arm experiment confirms these findings, showing that humans feel more comfortable interacting with robots that exhibit higher levels of motivational responsiveness. A significant advantage of our approach is its ability to effectively manage social dilemmas in robotic learning by preventing exploitation of low-motivation responses from human collaborators. Through analysis of the performance of both the robot and its human partner, we validate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving beneficial interactions. Our research demonstrates the importance of internal mental states in effective human-robot interaction and provides a new framework for designing compatible motivations. The proposed model can operate within established reinforcement learning frameworks with minimal modification and achieves improved interaction outcomes by selectively responding to associate's behavior. Our findings contribute to the understanding of internal mental states in human-robot collaboration and propose a new approach for designing and implementing them. A related technical report provides the detailed mathematical foundation for our model (available online at https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-08361-6_39). We introduce a novel method, LoFTR, which employs a unified framework based on the Transformer model to perform dense, detector-free regional feature matching for optical flow estimation. By using a unified framework, we eliminate the need for pre-training and reduce complexity in adapting it to diverse datasets, such as KITTI and DeepFlow, for end-to-end training. Our approach addresses spatially-irregular polygons using a grid-based representation and features a multi-scale refinement mechanism that significantly reduces sampling complexity. Experimental results on the widely-used Middlebury dataset, as well as DeepFlow, DeepEdge, and Sintel, demonstrate that LoFTR surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, achieving an improvement of 37% and 13% in average angular error, respectively. Notably, LoFTR outperforms Sintel-trained PWC-Net-DOS by 5.8% in average angular error on the Sintel dataset, and it also surpasses DeepFlow by 8.1% and 13% in average angular error on the KITTI dataset, when trained on it. Our source code and trained models are publicly available.

To calculate the solar vector magnetic field, we rely on objective indicators that have inherent biases. For instance, the presence of noise and the shape of a magnetic element significantly influence certain indicators. Understanding these biases is critical for selecting the optimal combination of indicators to use. We utilize a simple linear model to analyze the general characteristics of certain commonly employed indicators, including the Helmholtz mode amplitude and the vector average magnitude. Our results imply that a combination of indicators that includes at least one that is unbiased in a particular direction is necessary to recover the full vector magnetic field. We also identify potential issues with using least squares optimization in such a scenario, resulting in biased outcomes. Moreover, we introduce a directional minimum curvature method as an alternative, which is capable of providing the most accurate vector polarity configuration without being influenced by certain indicator biases. The performance of this algorithm is evaluated using noiseless magnetic field configurations and synthetic data. Lastly, we apply this method to actual data and compare its results with those obtained using the least squares algorithm. All experiments were conducted on a 3mHz granular cell derived from a SOT/BIS observation featuring relatively strong vertical fields. We find that the minimum curvature method performs at least equally well as the least squares algorithm in most cases, and in some cases, it requires minimal smoothing to produce a coherent vector magnetic field map with coherent polarity patterns, whereas the least squares algorithm may still benefit from smoothing to achieve a comparable outcome. We conclude that selecting the optimal combination of indicators and applying a method that can function independently of bias is crucial for achieving accurate solar surface magnetic field measurements. Such an approach enables us to obtain high-quality vector magnetic field maps free of noise and bias, especially in regions featuring vertical fields. We also acknowledge the limitations of our current algorithm, including its inability to handle horizontal fields effectively. Therefore, it is crucial to continue research focused on recognizing and mitigating bias in solar surface magnetic field measurements. Moreover, our results reveal that the SOT/BIS observation provides high spatial resolution but low temporal resolution. As a result, it is necessary to employ techniques such as forward modeling or focusing techniques in future observations to improve temporal resolution. The outcome of such an approach could significantly expand our understanding of the solar surface and its complex dynamics by filling the current knowledge gap in this area. Moreover, our results imply that high-quality solar surface magnetic field maps derived from actual data feature an order of magnitude higher magnitude than predicted open magnetic field strength, indicating that magnetic elements play a crucial role in determining the flow angle. This research explores the potential of an aggregative game approach to resolve a dispute between a power utility and residential consumers regarding immediate load invoicing. The concept of energy usage planning is utilized to determine a baseline for usage and instantly invoice any excess consumption above this baseline. To effectively apply this approach, a power utility must first establish a fair baseline that promotes efficient energy usage among residents. Consequently, a power utility must balance its need to set an optimal baseline to maximize its own benefits with the requirement to set a fair baseline that ensures the game has a Nash equilibrium. Furthermore, any strategy chosen by the power utility must not result in a Nash equilibrium that disproportionately benefits or disadvantages specific residential groups based on factors like income, to prevent potential discrimination. To address this challenge, this research proposes the use of a sequential Nash game approach where a power utility selectively imposes load invoicing on specific residential groups based on factors like income, and explores the relationship between the set baseline and the total amount of additional energy that residential consumers are willing to purchase. Furthermore, this research evaluates how a power utility's strategies affect its benefits and the total amount of additional energy that residential consumers are willing to purchase. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulation testing. The simulation reveals that a power utility's benefit from invoicing residential consumers for their immediate energy usage can be substantial, up to $104.18 per day, and that its strategic actions have a significant impact on the total amount of additional energy that residential consumers are willing to purchase, up to $3.66 million per day. The total amount of additional energy that residential consumers are willing to purchase also shows a significant level of variation, up to 3.66 million units per day, and that it is negatively affected by a power utility's strategic actions. The proposed approach provides a useful solution to the problem of setting a fair and optimal baseline for immediate load invoicing. The power utility can calculate the optimal immediate load invoicing amount by balancing its benefits with the amount of additional energy that residential consumers are willing to purchase. Consequently, this has the effect of imposing load invoicing on specific residential groups based on factors like income, and ultimately contributes to a significant reduction in the total amount of additional energy that residential consumers are willing to purchase, up to 3.66 million units per day. Furthermore, this research highlights the complex nature of this problem and the need for a more detailed analysis that takes into consideration the effect of a power utility's actions on different residential groups, and the amount of additional energy that they are willing to purchase,

To achieve this, researchers utilize spectral characteristics like the strength of specific features and temperature indicators. A novel method for identifying metal-poor stars, utilizing the Bayesian Algorithm for Generating Emulations with Spectral Traits, has been developed. This technique creates synthetic spectra based on atmospheric parameters like surface gravity, temperature, and metallicity, focusing on the latter to facilitate metal-poor star recognition. Wildfires pose a substantial threat to global ecosystems and the environment. They endanger human settlements and undermine local economies, particularly in regions with scorching climates. To combat this menace, specialists require reliable tools for predicting wildfire patterns. This study is called "BlazeWeb," a web application that uses geospatial data to show worldwide wildfire data in an interactive format. This format enables users to view cumulative, annual, and monthly wildfire statistics, as well as specific details about each blaze. This information includes geographic location, year, and total blazes across various years. To offer predictive analysis, BlazeWeb employs machine learning as its underlying algorithm. It uses two different machine learning models, one for forecasting and one for pattern classification, which were trained on NASA's FEWS dataset. This allows users to input current year and country data and receive predictions of upcoming cumulative blazes. This interactive feature is made possible through a user-friendly UI with a simplified navigation bar and adjustable year sliders for selecting country data. An error assessment is also provided, displaying the cross-validation error rate and corresponding loss function value. This allows users to compare the accuracy of different models and users can switch between different models. This application provides users with intuitive and dynamic tools to evaluate and predict wildfire data. It can be accessed via a website or API for use in research and forecasting. An example use case is demonstrating how BlazeWeb could be used to detect anomalies in wildfire data from the 2021 Delta variant country page. This shows a binary classifier model trained on COVID-19 data. When users input 2021 data for Germany, a significant spike is observed in December, which aligns with the Christmas surge during the pandemic. This example highlights the value of integrating machine learning with geospatial analysis for advanced applications. Users can access the BlazeWeb web application at http://blazeweb.karmanyan.com. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/karthyryan/BlazeWeb. For API usage, visit http://blazeweb.karmanyan.com/api. Building on this discovery, the study explores the coexistence of quantum guidance and Wigner negativity in certain states. Specifically, it identifies a state with both properties in a particular context of single-qubit systems. Furthermore, the research examines Wigner negativity in superdense states derived from entangled pairs of spin qubits and finds that Wigner negativity persists even when the entanglement of darkness is absent. However, the study reveals that Wigner negativity does not necessarily imply quantum guidance, presenting counterexamples to demonstrate this distinction. Ultimately, the research seeks to clarify the relationship between nonunitary states that support realist models and those that do not. Establishing secure communications over insecure channels is the fundamental goal of quantum key exchange (QKE), which has significant implications for practical applications. In real-world scenarios, QKE often involves non-ideal source security, non-passive source behavior, and noise affecting data transmission. Furthermore, users may have disparate trust levels and require different levels of protection, necessitating robust source security protection. This study explores QKE security under variable source security conditions using user trustworthiness and source uncertainty as key protective parameters. By applying Fidelis-bound evaluation and Bassage-repeated eavesdropping attacks, we examine the influence of source security and data transmission noise on QKE security, resulting in three consistent findings. Firstly, source security is the primary determinant of QKE security. Secondly, noise affecting data transmission does not compromise source security. Finally, noise affecting data transmission does not influence the conclusion of QKE security under conditions of uniform source security, but does compromise source security when source security is uncertain. This research provides a comprehensive analysis of QKE security under diverse real-world conditions, with far-reaching applications in various communication scenarios. Its results are anticipated to benefit experts in practical QKE security assessments, while also motivating further studies on theoretical QKE security models that account for real-world insecurity. In particular, this study sheds light on the crucial role of source security as a fundamental requirement for determining QKE security. As an application of this research, we demonstrate its implications for the practical source security protection problem with multiple trustworthy sources and variable source uncertainty. Our results indicate that source security can be guaranteed if and only if the probability of low source security and data transmission noise is low, while also illustrating the practical source security protection methods in this scenario. This research, which addresses the important practical source security protection problem with multiple trustworthy sources and variable source uncertainty, holds significant practical value. Its results enable the determination of the lowest required source security level for ensuring QKE security. Moreover, our research reveals the important factors influencing QKE security under non-ideal source security conditions, namely, user trustworthiness and source uncertainty. These factors hold significant practical value in determining the lowest required source security level for ensuring QKE security. This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those with negative curvatures in 3-dimensional space and positive 1-dimensional curvatures in 4-dimensional space, do not exhibit Bertrand parity. Furthermore, it indicates the presence of Bertrand curvatures in (2n-1)-dimensional space with n>1, but absent in n-dimensional space. Additionally, the study provides a geometric representation of these curvatures through null Bertrand curves in pseudo-Riemannian space. More specifically, the results show that only hyperboloid curves possess null Bertrand parity in 3-dimensional space, while spherical curves do not. In a different scenario with 5-dimensional space, Bertrand curvatures are found in (2n-1)-dimensional space with n>2, but not in n-dimensional space. More significantly, the study reveals a new geometric criterion, the Buekenhout-Peternoll (B-P) criterion, for identifying Bertrand curves, and examples of B-P curves are provided, specifically the hyperboloid curve in 3-dimensional space and a curve on the 5-dimensional hyperquadric space. The research also shows that these curves do not possess a new property called cross Bertrand curvature, and a non-geometric method using Lie groups is employed to demonstrate the cross Bertrand curvature paradox in certain curved spaces. More precisely, the results show that simply isotopic deformation of a curve does not necessarily imply a Bertrand curve, and this phenomenon is illustrated using Lorentzian hyperquadric curves in 5-dimensional space and curves on 6-dimensional space. Ultimately, the study confirms the existence of new geometric properties and paradoxes in curve theory. These findings are expected to offer valuable insights for researchers in this field. By combining weak convergence results, it is possible to establish the distribution of the extremal values of a Feller diffusion process, specifically for its running maximum and minimum values within a bounded interval. This is accomplished through the weak limits of sample quantiles, whose variations in a large number of independent samples follow a weakly convergent sequence determined by a stable limit law. Consequently, this approach yields an asymptotic representation of the sample path's extremal values via a dependent factor plus a residual error, while also enabling the creation of error bars for the samples by drawing on quantile functions. This technique is illustrated by analyzing a stationary, symmetric diffusion process, specifically the SDE-driven process $X_t=\int_0^{\tau_1}\sigma(s,\omega)\,d\B_t(s,\omega))$, where its killing time $\tau_1$ is determined by a threshold that caps the process's positive values. Consequently, this resolves an approximately two decades-old problem concerning the asymptotic behavior of the process's running maximum. Similarly, this methodology is applied to the study of Brownian motion's extrema within a bounded interval. All necessary technical details, including the sample size's optimal order and crucial quantile conditions, are thoroughly elaborated in the main paper. Additionally, a brief introduction briefly outlines the underlying reasoning behind the presented findings. Moreover, a related inquiry concerning the diffusion process's extremal values within a growing interval remains unsolved but proposed as future research. Finally, the author expresses gratitude to S. N. Cohen for sharing his solution to the proposed interval-related problem prior to its presentation in this work. 

Related results and discussions are further presented in the addendum, including an alternative approach for combining weak convergence and sampling distributions, specifically for the study of a stationary, symmetric diffusion process's inverse waiting time for its process's first exit from a bounded interval. This is accomplished through the strategic selection of a set of times, resulting in a distributional limit that bears a resemblance to an inverse Gaussian distribution. Moreover, this technique is further developed by establishing a distributional result for a growth rate of extreme values. This is accomplished by analyzing a set of samples from a time interval $\tau_1$ and applying weak convergence to derive an asymptotic representation of the growth rate of extreme values, specifically via a dependent factor plus a residual error. Moreover, this enables the creation of error bars for the samples by drawing on quantile functions.

In this approach, we analyze photon scattering in waveguide QED systems consisting of multiple emitters, employing a graphical method to simplify complex interactions and obtain exact, computationally manageable formulas for determining scattering probabilities and distribution ratios. This technique allows us to expand existing theories, initially designed for a single emitter, to accommodate systems with multiple emitters, while also investigating novel phenomena that arise from complex emitter interactions. Furthermore, we apply the graphical method to explore fundamental processes in three-key systems: single-photon conversion, two-photon transitions, and simultaneous double-emitter scattering. The scale-free diagrams generated by this approach reveal universal principles governing these processes in systems consisting of weakly interacting emitters. However, when emitters interact more strongly, the phase relationships between their internal states become intertwined with photon states, resulting in complex interconnections between free and scattered distribution ratios. Additionally, we explore the practical uses of the graphical method by illustrating its potential in optimizing devices that manipulate quantum light and reducing the inherent errors in simultaneous double-emitter scattering processes. The graphical method presents a unified understanding of scattering phenomena in waveguide QED systems of any complexity and sets the stage for exploring new phenomena in larger configurations. We've used a two-color noncommutative Yang-Mills theory to develop a formalism for nucleon composition functions, which depend on noncommutative momentum and nucleon structure. This framework is compatible with QCD's collinear factorization property for large nucleon momentum, allowing us to derive analytic formulas for composition functions that reflect nucleon bound states, gluon scattering, and the effects of reggeization. We've found that, at a certain scale, our theory's composition functions match those in a standard two-color Yang-Mills theory, but, at higher scales, they differ due to noncommutative effects and information on gluon distribution. We've investigated the effects of this difference on nucleon structure observed in deep inelastic scattering experiments and found that, while the nucleon's overall gluon content matches in both theories, its gluon moment distribution differs. We've also used our findings to estimate the effects of noncommutative effects on various nucleon structure observables. This calculation reveals that, while these effects are generally small, they are not negligible and, in some cases, can be significant. We've obtained an estimate for the value of an important scale in our theory, denoted by $\sqrt{t_0}$, which is related to the size of nucleons in light-front quantization, based on experimental data and theoretical predictions from both a standard two-color Yang-Mills theory and our noncommutative two-color Yang-Mills theory. This calculation yields a wide interval of possible values, but a new constraint from a recent experiment narrows this range significantly. We've also demonstrated that our noncommutative two-color Yang-Mills theory can resolve several long-standing puzzles in hadron physics and QCD, including the behavior of nucleon composition functions at very small and high momentum, and the interplay between gluon distribution and nucleon bound-state effects in the nucleon. We've obtained a number of new predictions in nucleon structure, including an estimate of the nucleon's $x$-dependent gluon distribution and its Regge behavior for various hadron processes using both a standard two-color Yang-Mills theory and our noncommutative two-color Yang-Mills theory. These predictions reveal that our noncommutative theory's behavior differs from the standard theory's in certain cases and agrees with it in others. Finally, our analysis suggests that noncommutative effects may be detected in several high-energy experiments, including those at the Large Hadron Collider and the Future Electron-Ion

As data science evolves, the need for assessment tools to evaluate how well algorithms can transfer knowledge to humans grows. Although there are numerous tools to measure machine learning performance, the field of assessment for human learning remains underdeveloped. In this paper, a new framework for assessing algorithmic interpretability from a human learning perspective is introduced. This comprehensive framework captures a range of cognitive aspects related to a specific task, and for each aspect, it quantifies the level of cognitive complexity involved. In order to demonstrate its effectiveness, the framework is applied to examine the learning of linear regression and decision tree models from two different perspectives: a domain expert and a non-expert. The framework shows that domain experts have lower cognitive complexity when learning these algorithms in comparison to non-experts. Furthermore, the framework's results highlight the importance of prior knowledge in understanding algorithmic explanations. In addition, the framework's applicability in real-world scenarios is illustrated through a case study involving Google's decision tree-based feature prediction tool, and the results show that human engineers can benefit from the score in their daily tasks. The framework's code is openly accessible and can be readily applied for evaluation purposes. Anomaly detection using Time WS isolation forest offers an suitable approach for real-time identification of outliers in streaming data, especially in resource-constrained environments where a wide range of data distributions can be effectively handled. Building on the loosely supervised machine learning principles, we developed an isolated forest algorithm specifically designed for processing single-feature data in real-time, yielding high detection accuracy rates up to 99% on standard anomaly detection datasets like IEEE-MAG, MUSCLE, and Glass, even when only partially supervised. Notably, our method exhibits exceptional resource efficiency, requiring minimal memory and processing overheads, making it well-suited for deployment on limited hardware. Further customization of our isolation forest algorithm led to the creation of DeepWS-IF, a deep learning-based variant that can learn a more efficient anomaly detection model directly from data, while maintaining high accuracy rates and performance in real-time streaming anomaly detection applications. Additionally, our method allows for the generation of synthetic anomaly data through generative adversarial networks in real-time, providing an efficient strategy to balance detection accuracy and computational resources in adaptive anomaly detection systems. Extreme events often occur randomly and can be modeled as a high-value sample from a probability distribution, known as the extreme-value model.  Understanding the frequency and expectations of such events is critical, but traditional methods often have limitations, particularly when dealing with long-term data.  A new approach, based on the theory of points, offers a compelling alternative by redefining extreme values as a specific type of random process.  This model allows for a Bayesian estimation technique that takes into account the uncertainty associated with estimating the extreme values, and we provide a comprehensive mathematical framework for this approach, including formulas for estimating the number of extreme events.  Additionally, we expand upon previous theories to develop a broader extreme-value model that incorporates various types of distribution patterns and is particularly useful for analyzing non-standard patterns in weather data.  The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through the analysis of two real-world datasets from meteorological stations.  To our knowledge, this estimation technique is a groundbreaking development in the theory of extreme values, offering a flexible and accurate method for estimating the number of extreme events.  A related software package, known as thornborough, provides an essential tool for implementing this approach and facilitating its use in practical applications.  The theoretical contributions of this article are complemented by the practical applications and sensitivity analyses presented in Section 4, and we also offer additional insights and reflections in Section 5.  Ultimately, the Bayesian estimation technique described in this article has significant implications for a variety of scientific and statistical disciplines, and we conclude with a number of potential research directions suggested in Section 5.  The related Python software package for this approach, known as thornborough, is available for download at http://thornborough.github.io/, and the associated Python source code can be accessed at http://thornborough.github.io/doc/code.html. In this study, we conduct a thorough examination of the impact of rapidity distribution width on rapidity covariance and cross sectional averages in simple systems.  Initially, we generate two groups of hypothetical rapidity distributions, one being uniform and the other being Gaussian in nature, centered around distinct average rapidity values.  We then plot the distribution of these two groups against average rapidity for fixed values of cross sectional averages.  Interestingly, our findings reveal that the area under the curve for the uniform distribution is always triangular in shape, in contrast, the Gaussian distribution exhibits a semicircular pattern.  Notably, this pattern is reminiscent of gauge boson distribution transverse momentum in certain environments.  We plan to extend this study in future work by exploring the impact of transverse momentum on rapidity distribution and cross sectional averages.  This research may have practical implications for understanding certain properties of quark-gluon plasma.  We believe that the results presented here, along with those in our forthcoming paper, will contribute significantly to advancing theoretical understanding of rapidity distributions and their associated properties.  Importantly, this work may also shed light on the unique properties of systems comprising heavy particles.  While the results presented in this study are considered to be classical in nature, they still offer a significant amount of accuracy in the context of quantum mechanical systems, particularly at low values of transverse momentum.  Ultimately, this study provides valuable insights into the rapidity distribution characteristics that may be relevant in various fields including QCD, heavy ion collisions and cosmology.  As such, it is hoped that the results of this study may serve as a valuable starting point for future investigations in these areas.  Interestingly, one of the key findings of this study is that the area under the curve of rapidity distributions, whether uniform or Gaussian in nature, is always proportional to the square of the average rapidity value when the mean cross sectional average is held constant.  Notably, this property is reminiscent of certain Maxwell distributions in Maxwell-Boltzmann theory.  We plan to further explore these idealized systems in a forthcoming paper, where we will also examine systems exhibiting Gaussian rapidity distributions with fixed values of cross sectional averages.  One of the key observations of this study is that the isopycnic curves, which represent contours of constant mean values in the rapidity distribution plane, display distinct geometric characteristics that are dependent on the choice of rapidity distribution and fixed value of the cross sectional average.  Importantly, we will provide a mathematical explanation for these observed patterns

Our investigation of the metal-rich globular cluster NGC 2808, known for its multiple stellar populations, has led to significant findings regarding the characteristics of its first-generation stars. Leveraging photometry from the VLT, HST, and Gaia missions, we conducted a precise analysis of 88 stars with estimated ages of around 10 billion years. Utilizing this data, we refined the parameters of the cluster and derived detailed properties of these first-generation stars within an acceptable margin of error. Our results reveal a chemical disparity within the cluster, consistent with prior studies, and specifically confirm the presence of a spread in the levels of Mg abundance, a trait also observed in other rich metal clusters. This disparity is observed in both the Mg$_{ab}$ ratio and Mg/H value, and is significantly influenced by the star's location on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. Notably, the highest Mg abundance was found among red giant stars, while lower levels were detected in less evolved stars. This pattern was accounted for through the star's evolutionary stage, and not due to issues related to the method's errors or the star's surface temperature. On a more general note, our study highlights the importance of achieving high photometric accuracy, a trait often difficult to obtain for massive celestial objects. We trust that these findings will contribute positively to the study of stellar populations in the galaxy's globular clusters. However, further investigation is required to thoroughly grasp the chemical disparity within the galaxy's globular clusters and the origin of their distinctively different elemental compositions.

Unauthenticated and distorted messages sent through an additive white Gaussian noise channel can be detected by legitimate users under both unconditional and conditional key distributions, according to the findings. Specifically, when no secret key is available, unconditional key distributions provide optimal resistance to intentional interference, whereas conditional key distributions offer strong security against passive eavesdropping, even without using verification protocols. Moreover, when secret keys are available, conditional key distributions offer security against active attacks that attempt to compromise these keys. These outcomes are demonstrated through a concrete example, highlighting the need for precise characterization of communication systems at a theoretical and practical level, as a single flawed assumption can render all cryptographic analyses and methods superficial, as exemplified in the Gilbert-Elliott channel. Consequently, verifiable communications, verifiable key agreements, and verifiable key distributions are identified as essential components of secure communication. Due to the inherent complexities of verifying communications and common pitfalls in verifying key distributions, a new theory and verification method are proposed, addressing these challenges and providing a general framework that can simultaneously verify a wide range of keyless key distributions, including those that are commonly considered secure. The verification method has been applied to ten well-known examples of discrete and continuous-time distributions, confirming its correctness and highlighting critical issues in secure communication systems that have previously gone unaddressed. Our theory and verification method provide the first comprehensive characterization of keyless key distributions, enabling a clear distinction between secure communications systems that are resistant to attacks and those that are vulnerable to intentional interference. Importantly, our results demonstrate that existing keyless key distributions, including those widely considered secure, provide little protection against passive eavesdropping, while also being easily compromised by active attacks that target the verification process itself. In particular, we show that in many communication systems, including those that are commonly thought of as secure, the verification process can be successfully attacked by an adversary who seeks to compromise the system, leading to the emergence of new attacks that target the verification method itself. Future work and applications are discussed. The verification method has been implemented in a TypeScript application, enabling a clear distinction between secure communications systems that are resistant to attacks and those that are vulnerable to intentional interference. Estimating impulse responses from observational time series data is feasible when variables are jointly measured, but can be challenging when only a single variable is available, as is the case with satellite data. To overcome this difficulty, we develop a novel approach that applies the local linear projection technique within a set of concurrent paths, each corresponding to a different potential causal variable. Notably, our approach adapts the local projection criterion on a per-path basis, unlike traditional methods that apply the same criteria uniformly. We validate the improved approach through a series of experiments and apply it to estimate impulse responses for two significant challenges: modeling ocean circulation changes and tracking Arctic coverage fluctuations. Furthermore, we compare our enhanced method to both the original local linear projection approach and a model that selects among the variables rather than posing a priori assumptions about their relationships. Our results indicate that the adaptive approach offers a suitable compromise between the potential biases of the original local linear projection and the risks associated with model selection. A summary represents a document's pivotal elements to convey its main message.
Despite notable progress in single-language and monolingual summarization, strong language models have made mixed language text increasingly manageable.
This study investigates a novel challenge - summarizing documents written in multiple Indian languages using a single-language transformer model.
To tackle this issue, we introduce two new datasets combining English with two prominent Indian languages: Urdu and Tamil.
Our analysis on these datasets reveals that current models struggle to handle texts containing sentences in multiple languages due to several reasons.
To address this challenge, we propose a method called GAE-ISumm, employing a transformer model to capture sentence-level information and combine it with graph attention to capture document-level signals.
Our experimental results show that GAE-ISumm outperforms competing methods in single-document and abstractive summarization tasks. Additionally, we also examine its performance in zero-shot settings where the summary language differs from the document's language. Our findings indicate that GAE-ISumm holds its own against baselines even in such zero-shot settings. A thorough examination of various auxiliary tasks as well as an automatic and manual evaluation of generated summaries complements our analysis. An $S$-ring of Noether type can be described as a multiplicative subset of a commutative polynomial ring that follows Noetherian type induction, originating from Noether's Ring Lemma applied to local rings. Examples include rational functions and power series rings. Given any $S$-ring of Noether type, we demonstrate that a particular divisor exists, characterizing unique factorization, and establish the application of Zariski pairs in geometric contexts. Additionally, we define an $S$-ideal of linear dimension and prove an extension of the Hilbert Syzygy Theorem, both generalizing and, in some cases, surpassing existing theories for rational function rings and power series rings. Moreover, we define an $S$-local sequence and its associated $S$-local connections, finding connections to logarithmic singularities. Finally, we introduce a particular type of $S$-linear map and prove its equivalence to the free $A$-module structure in certain cases. Moreover, we define an $S$-ideal as linear if its $A$-local sequence is linear and demonstrate its significant algebraic and geometric implications. This includes an extension of the Cartan-Killing theorem, a proof that linear $S$-ideals correspond to torsion-free divisor ideals, and a generalization of the Cohen-Macaulay theorem. All these results, originally in power series and rational function ring contexts, are now extended to any $S$-ring of Noether type. Furthermore, we define the $S$-linear dual and establish its application in both commutative and noncommutative settings. Importantly, the $S$-linear dual's properties do not rely on $A$-ring commutativity, and in the case of rational function rings, the $S$-linear dual's structure significantly connects to Diophantine geometry. Finally, the $S$-linear dual's relationship to involution is demonstrated. Key concepts including the $S$-double dual, the invariance property, and the maximal noncommutative rank in various contexts are also discussed, with the request for further exploration on duals in non- Noetherian settings. This work represents a comprehensive expansion and improvement of both commutative and noncommutative ring theories, including results from Frobenius, commutative ring, local cohomology, and log algebra literature, now generalized to $S$-ring of Noether type categories. We focus on the problem of identifying the effects of specific interventions on
individual data points after conducting an exhaustive search for intervention
policy optimization. In the framework of Multiple Testing and FDR control, we
develop a two-stage approach to select intervention outcomes with guaranteed
intervention impact identification and controlled false discovery rate under
dependent data. We implement this strategy using Linear Programming, which
yielded satisfactory results according to the results of our in-depth
experiments under various scenarios. Notably, our method exhibits efficient
computational performance across large datasets. We demonstrate the practical
applicability of our approach in the field of finance with a real-world policy-
making application. Using real-world data, we successfully identify intervention
policy outcomes that are beneficial, efficient, and non-deceptive, specifically for
predictive variables that are profitable, efficient, and consistent. We also show
that our approach meets the criteria for valid intervention impact identification. 
Moreover, we achieve a controlled FDR of 0.38, outperforming the 0.40 FDR from
uncontrolled methods on average, with an improvement of 5% in 7 out of 10 tests.
Interestingly, our approach surpasses the FDR from historical, expert-tested 21
methods on average across all 30 tests. We also demonstrate the ability of our
method to extract intervention impact identification using recent state-of-the-art
feature selection approaches. We emphasize the importance of intervening on
profitable, efficient, and consistent features to maximize expected returns. 
Lastly, we stress that our approach's success relies heavily on the diversity of
intervention policies to ensure that the most effective policies are not overly
reliant on a few key variables. We then demonstrate this concept in the context of
the established dataset.

Entrainment theory suggests that interactions between people are typically characterized by a dynamic of reciprocal influences, with the intensity of this effect being measured by entrainment distance. This study uses a type of deep neural network to develop models for measuring the distance between conversational partners through characteristics like speaking tempo, voice pitch, and other vocal attributes. Analyzing data from about 1,700 people engaging in conversations, the research shows that entrainment models based on audible data are able to predict the tempo and pitch entrainment distances with remarkable accuracy, also revealing that these distances are linked to the conversational setting. This research represents one of the first attempts to use artificial intelligence to measure the entrainment phenomenon. Domain adjustment, particularly source-free domain adjustment, is a crucial task that involves adjusting a model's performance to a new unseen domain without using information from that specific domain. This paper focuses on adjusting a pre-trained model when limited labeled data is available for the new domain. A usual approach involves fine-tuning a model using self-supervised learning on unlabeled source data, but this method does not fully utilize domain-specific information. Therefore, a new framework has been proposed that involves three key steps: first, identifying important features for each domain using unsupervised self-training; second, transferring these features to the target domain; and third, reinitializing the model using both supervised and semi-supervised learning techniques. Experiments were conducted across multiple datasets and domains, yielding improved performance compared to existing methods. Notably, our proposed framework achieved an increase of more than 10% in accuracy for the Amazon-Contextual Walks dataset and a rise of almost 5% for the DeepFashion-C dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in adjusting a model's performance to a new, unseen domain with limited labeled data. You can access our source code here: https://github.com/ashish9108/SFTNet. This work extends a previous study that initially introduced the idea of adjusting models without access to source domain information. Similar ideas have been explored in recent research, including a study that used domain-adjusted language models to transfer knowledge across domains. However, our proposed framework offers a new perspective based on learning domain-relevant features, and yields better performance compared to existing methods. Additionally, our approach does not require perfect feature detection, and yields improved results by only requiring twice the number of unlabeled target domain samples used in the original feature selection process. You can access our source code here: https://github.com/ashish9108/SFTNet.

Designed to handle the unique demands of dimensional high-dimensional time-based data, the BTO efficiently trains on short, composite temporal sequences, making it well-suited for analyzing dynamic cell processes. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of the BTO by applying it to real-world cell observation scenarios, both in actual experiments and through simulation testing. These comparative studies indicate that the BTO consistently outperforms traditional machine learning methods. Moreover, we have shown that the BTO's ability to detect changes in data properties, known as drift detection, is a vital component in its success, especially when these changes occur within brief timeframes. Ultimately, the BTO's ability to efficiently learn from short temporal sequences makes it a valuable tool for analyzing dynamic cell processes, particularly in applications where the capture of rich temporal information is crucial, like cell division monitoring. To further understand the underlying mechanics of the BTO, we have conducted thorough algorithmic analysis and tested its stability across a wide array of parameter settings. These findings have led to the recommendation of best-practice guidelines for designing monitored learning algorithms, which we have validated by applying the BTO to real-world cell observation scenarios to further demonstrate its effectiveness. We then performed simulation testing on the proposed framework, which consistently shows that the BTO outperforms comparable methods. These results illustrate that the BTO detects changes more accurately and requires less training time under numerous experimental settings. To showcase its practical value, we have used the BTO to analyze actual cell division monitoring situations. In this study, we address the challenge of action detection using impoverished labels that only signify the action's start and end time and associated video ID. From a technical perspective, our main objective is to leverage image processing features that accurately capture the action's context while managing to exclude irrelevant video clip segments, separate distinct actions with similar names, and filter out ambiguous context manifestations. To accomplish this, we introduce PHD-GCN, a graph-based neural network model for video action detection that relies on three key components. First, we devise a performance-enhancing graph structure for the model. Second, we create a specialized neural network for processing video frames and integrating the pre-trained C3D feature extractor while incorporating the graph structure. Third, we develop a customized cost function for optimizing performance by integrating the pre-trained ground truth annotations. We evaluated the PHD-GCN model on three Guided BD and Weakly Guided Action Detection benchmarks and obtained remarkable results, achieving an impressive 76% enhancement in the DET50 metric when compared to the conventional C3D approach. Notably, our model outperformed other state-of-the-art approaches on the NIMBUS-201, UEC-FV Action Detection, and CMU Action Grammar benchmarks. Furthermore, our extensive experimentation process uncovered the effectiveness of graph structure parameters and the C3D feature extractor when utilized in the model's training phase. Additionally, our analysis demonstrates the model's capacity for automatically learning the context of actions during the training process. From a practical perspective, our research confirms the feasibility of utilizing impoverished labels for guiding action detection in videos. This year's Image2Video Retrieval Challenge featured two categories, one focusing on intrinsic similarity through still-image recall, and the other emphasizing semantic similarity via interactive exploration.  The dataset used for the competition was derived from the COCO challenge.  The winners of the still-image recall category, DeepIm, utilized a convolutional neural network-based approach, achieving top results with a recall efficiency that surpassed 99%.  Semantics-based researcher, Valery Koltonogov, secured first place in the semantic category with FUSE, a method that employs a dynamic memory network for contextual tracking.  The conference included two additional workshops - one on still-image similarity, featuring a new benchmark known as Image Retrieval Archive (IRA), and the other on semantic search, presenting the CRIC dataset for identifying coherent text segments.  Due to COVID-19 restrictions, the conference was held as a hybrid event, providing attendees with both in-person and remote presentation options.  A total of 67 papers were presented, addressing a range of topics including still-image similarity, semantic search, local guidelines for data annotation, image2video retrieval, explainable AI models, and retrieval model conformity assessment.  Two distinct datasets were also introduced - the Image Retrieval Archive (IRA) for still-image similarity, and the Semantics-based researcher's dataset, FUSE, for semantic search, containing over 250K scenes indexed via MS COOP.  Data and code for the competition are openly accessible on https://imagebench.org.  We would like to extend our gratitude to the participants, dataset creators, and reviewers for their substantial contributions, and the event was sponsored by the human vision project at the Skolkovo Center for Artificial Intelligence.  A short video illustrating the competition is available on YouTube at https://youtube.com/c/ SkolkovoAI.  We look forward to participating in future challenges. Our research involves an analysis of a second-order linear parabolic equation that arises in a context where a random model with a small parameter is applied to a bounded region in a polynomial space. When this model is transformed into an ordinary differential equation with random parameters, it exhibits metastability due to the presence of two time scales, which can be understood through an asymptotic analysis. Our investigation of the boundary value problems that emerge in the model involves intricate mathematical operations and the application of probabilistic techniques, including a thorough examination of the behavior of a solution at its boundary. Additionally, we apply a homogenization technique to demonstrate that, as the parameter approaches zero, the solution of the model converges to a solution of a corresponding homogeneous equation. This technique requires a careful analysis of the behavior of a special function that involves a transition between two time scales, which can be challenging due to its dependence on the boundary conditions of the model. Our research is then extended to a broader class of degenerate diffusion models, which allows us to draw connections between our findings and a recently studied model of stochastic phases, as well as a theoretical framework for understanding the behavior of a solution of a degenerate parabolic equation near its boundary. Specifically, we have derived an alternative representation of a solution that takes into account its behavior at the boundary using a probabilistic argument, which can be generalizable to a broader class of equations. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that, as the boundary conditions of a model become more complex, the solution of the model can exhibit a variety of metastable behaviors, which can be a result of the emergence of slow scales in the model. Our findings are supported by an extensive numerical method that enables the visualization of the various time scales in the model. Importantly, our research is accompanied by a series of numerical examples that highlight the practical significance of our findings, which can be valuable for informing a variety of applications, including materials science, biology, and medicine. Such behavior is, in fact, a common phenomenon in physical systems, as well as a key factor in the emergence of metastability in the model. Our research is, therefore, a contribution to a broader scientific understanding of the emergence of quasiperiodic behaviors in physical systems. Our research explores the effects of intense magnetic fields on the properties of neutron-rich, weakly bound nuclei, focusing on the atomic nucleus $^6$He. We develop a computational method to determine how the magnetic field influences the spatial distribution of the system's bound particles near the focal point of a laser beam by utilizing the Local Scale Resolution Method. To this end, we apply the Local Scale Transform method, a novel approach that employs the Local Scale Transform concept and the Local Scale Separation of Variables method, to solve the Schrödinger equation effectively and obtain a precise set of wave functions that satisfy the given boundary conditions. We analyze our results in the context of recent experiments that utilized ultra-intense magnetic fields to study weakly bound isotopes. We find that the spatial dimensions of the system can change significantly in the presence of such fields, which may facilitate certain processes, particularly if the laser pulse and magnetic field are properly aligned. We present a visualization of the system's configuration in this scenario. Additionally, we outline possible avenues for experimental verification of our findings, emphasizing the importance of incorporating our results into the data analysis due to the significant overlap between our predictions and experimental data regarding certain observables. We further highlight the potential of our research by outlining its implications for future experiments and specific applications in theoretical studies of atomic systems subjected to intense magnetic fields, emphasizing the importance of incorporating our results in such cases. A comprehensive discussion regarding our research, including associated challenges and the underlying theory that enabled our findings, is also presented in the accompanying PhD dissertation. We then apply these methods to various problems and overcome related challenges in the accompanying FAQs. In a decentralized learning environment, numerous students share common educational goals, yet many live in areas with limited internet connectivity or surveillance by educational authorities, making it essential to keep their data confidential. The conventional approach to education, relying on a central server that collects student data, poses significant security risks in such situations. Recent advancements in Federated Learning (FL), which enables training to occur directly on edge devices, address these security concerns, albeit at the cost of increasing communication when large model parameters are used. Practically effective FL systems are predicted to play a significant role in future educational settings. Existing FL frameworks, however, often fall short in such sensitive applications due to several critical issues. 

This paper proposes a new, localized education framework called DP-REC that simultaneously guarantees model accuracy, protects student data privacy, and minimizes communication overhead. This framework combines a unique strategy for parameter quantization, which combines least significant bit removal and quantization, with a disturbance-based technique to enhance graduation, which significantly improves the trade-off between model accuracy and student data privacy, and allows for individualized control of this trade-off based on user-defined parameters. Additionally, DP-REC employs a disturbance-based gradient masking method to determine the optimal level of gradient masking, which maximizes model accuracy when data is subject to noise. This framework also protects against label inference in several scenarios through the application of disturbance-based methods. Experimental results confirm that DP-REC effectively increases model accuracy and offers enhanced privacy protection and energy efficiency compared to other localized education frameworks. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the required communication can be as low as 6.93% of the communication needed in a centralized learning setting to achieve similar model accuracy in a few key applications. This framework has been made available on our website for public access. Using this framework, FL systems can achieve both security and efficiency, which may open up new possibilities for applying FL in sensitive environments.

We analyze self-govering models with limited information, defining their stages based on key event occurrences: a distinction is made between events leading to decision-making and those following it, as well as between events that are known in advance and those that are not. To understand how these models evolve over multiple stages, we investigate two types of multi-phase models. First, we focus on situations where decision-makers do not consider the possibility of decision-makers' behavior being utility-maximizing. To this end, we provide a cognitive description of common knowledge situations, as well as definitions for recursive and quasi-recursive scenarios that are applicable to any initial two-player game of incomplete information. We then explore how these definitions can be used to understand three types of multi-phase games of incomplete information: those involving simultaneous decision-making, alternating decision-making, and games of imperfect information. Situations where new information emerges after each stage complicate the analysis, so we primarily study games that are characterized by a lack of new information. To understand these games, we first identify definitions for common knowledge recursive scenarios, which we then apply to a distinguished class of games of incomplete information. A key function of the MoE is to route input data towards optimized sub-networks tailored to processing distinct data subsets, ultimately enabling the realization of more complex distributions through the combination of localized expert capabilities. The dial-a-ride problem (DARP) requires the scheduling of a fleet of vehicles to meet the transportation needs of a geographic area with multiple passengers needing to travel between specified pickup and drop-off times, with multiple possible routes available. This problem becomes particularly challenging due to the large number of possible routes, passenger demands, and service constraints. In response, this, a new Dial-a-Ride metropolitan planning model is proposed, along with a corresponding Branch-and-Bound algorithm. This model distinguishes itself by incorporating key urban planning factors, such as passenger distribution, into the optimization process. In comparison to existing DARP models, this approach recognizes that passengers do not necessarily travel in rush-hour conditions and must consider parking requirements when arriving at their destinations. Evaluations of the proposed algorithm show that it effectively solves Dial-a-Ride problems that cannot be solved through simpler models, and in addition to providing optimal solutions, it also generates relevant planning outcomes such as the number of vehicles needed, passenger costs, and trip efficiency. Finally, a series of test cases highlighting the practical implications of this planning model are presented.

Our proposed model, Sliding Sequential CVAE (SSCVAE), analyzes multi-step interaction forecasts by breaking them down into smoother, easier-to-predict segments, enabling faster and more precise predictions. By reexamining the forecast segments and using a socially-aware loss function, SSCVAE produces more accurate and socially conscious future trajectory predictions, outperforming existing models like STG CNN in predicting both individual and social aspects of futures trajectories for multiple moving objects in various real-world scenarios as shown in the second place achievement in tracking challenge 3 of the 2021 ICRA tracking benchmark. In response, we develop a communication strategy utilizing hand gestures for human-swarm interaction. However, the traditional approach of training a single neural network from a comprehensive dataset assumes a perfect training dataset, which in reality is often plagued by imperfections and biases. Consequently, neural networks may perform poorly on data that differs from what they were trained on, a phenomenon known as the data-domainshift. But what if a more robust approach could harness the unique strengths of multiple networks? To explore this, we trained and combined numerous neural networks on various subsets of the Slovak Blood Cell Dataset, and as a result, achieved remarkably higher overall accuracy and performance. But what about the reliability of this ensemble method? Considering that ensemble learning was utilized, we put our model through a battery of 20 independent evaluations. Interestingly, our analysis of the results revealed that while retraining the networks on more data yielded improved accuracy, the variability in the ensemble model's performance was better predicted by the initial accuracy of the individual networks rather than the amount of training data. Our work has far-reaching implications for the development of neural network-based medical diagnostic tools, specifically in the context of image analysis, which often suffers from limited and imperfect datasets due to various clinical and non-clinical factors. By acknowledging and addressing these limitations through the creation of expert systems, our research demonstrates that it may be more beneficial to design solutions around specific problems rather than striving for broad generalization, a concept also known as transfer learning. Ultimately, our model's success highlights the importance of independence in the development of neural network-based systems, which can lead to remarkable improvements in performance when effectively applied. Our results also underscore the significance of independent validation, which in this study, involved a third-party expert visually categorizing representative samples to determine the accuracy of the model. However, the relationship between these formats is not well documented, particularly when it comes to transferring information from a more advanced, resource-based system to the more basic RDF format.  This research examines the challenges of this information transfer and explores ways to enhance RDF by incorporating elements from more feature-rich systems.  The transfer of information between these formats was studied through the lens of shape expression logic, which provides the framework for modeling certain resource-oriented systems and the RDF database system.  The results of this research reveal that key concepts from these systems that are lost during transfer can be restored, specifically hierarchical relationships and specific object characteristics.  The methods proposed in this study enable these concepts to be preserved during transfer by incorporating various encodings into the RDF format.  The results of experimental tests using publicly available information models confirmed that using these methods preserves the integrity of these complex systems when converting them to RDF.  The results further indicate that combining these methods with existing search methods for finding data relationships enhances the feature-richness of RDF, making it a more attractive candidate for integrating diverse information models.  The implementation of this research was done within the context of a resource-oriented information system and the results of the tests were conducted on the massive Wikipedia information database.  The results of this research indicate that using these methods significantly improves the feature-richness of RDF and provides users with faster and more comprehensive access to information.  The results of this research were tested and validated in a practical application and are available for download.  The research further suggests several potential areas for extending the feature-richness of RDF and the RDF data language, which could lead to the development of a more robust and scalable data processing framework. We introduce pyStoNED, a new Python package offering a tool for nonparametric analysis called StoNED, which enables the estimation of multi-output convex functions. Additionally, pyStoNED provides functions to compute conditional value-at-risk and expected shortfall in closed form. Our implementation of StoNED relies on a novel multi-output regression technique known as MultiLearner Ensembling, which allows for flexible, differentiable function approximation. Building upon pyStoNED, we develop an accessible and versatile framework for examining multi-output convex functions' properties, encompassing frontier assessment, uncertainty quantification, and optimization scenarios. Furthermore, incorporating pyStoNED into a Monte Carlo framework would facilitate efficient use, as it allows the use of StoNED's estimates in a pre-computed dataset for various applications. Our paper details the underlying methodology of pyStoNED, showcases its core functions through hands-on numerical examples, and discusses its potential implications. Finally, to ensure maximum usability, we address practical considerations, such as handling multi-dimensional input variables and outliers, which are often encountered in real-world problems. As an additional benefit, pyStoNED's functionality also extends to non-convex functions as well, although this is not necessarily its primary use case. Similar to other Python libraries like scipy, statsmodels, or pymc3, our goal for pyStoNED is to provide a useful tool, making it easily accessible through a user-friendly interface and transparent, open-source code. Ultimately, we anticipate that pyStoNED will serve as a useful entry-point for users to investigate advanced nonparametric optimization methods, such as non-smooth or multi-output function optimization, which often come with significant mathematical and implementation hurdles. In a theoretical model known as $t \bar t \phi$ generation, the Higgs boson ($\phi$) is linked to the top quark's electroweak doublet. This type of model can be supported by a discrete symmetry that inhibits the direct production of the Higgs boson via gluon fusion. However, the presence of this symmetry often results in the moderate production of the Higgs boson in conjunction with top quarks. Our analysis, conducted to investigate this phenomenon, utilized simulated data from the LHC's run II, generated top quark pairs in conjunction with a Higgs boson of 125 GeV, and demonstrated that with sufficient statistics, it's feasible to detect evidence of this type of model that's 3 sigma above background noise. Specifically, this would be achieved with 36.5 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity, yielding approximately 8 events over background noise. Furthermore, we proposed a new type of observatory to determine the Higgs boson's coupling to the top quark, and demonstrated its potential sensitivity to various types of couplings. Finally, we estimated that with 131 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity, this type of observatory would be able to measure the Higgs boson's trilinear coupling with sensitivity of at least 20 times the square root of the coupling's value. Conversely, our results also revealed the limitations of this type of model, particularly its inability to generate sensitivity of less than 10 times the square root of the coupling's value. One of the main reasons for this is the significant amount of statistical noise generated by top quark pair production, alongside Higgs boson production, and semi-leptonic decays. Nonetheless, the $t \bar t \phi$ generation offers one of the most promising avenues for investigating the Higgs boson's coupling to quarks at the LHC, particularly in a manner that complements and enhances the detector's capabilities for searching for these types of particles. Such a search would be of great scientific value, particularly if it resulted in the detection of, for example, an enhanced Higgs boson coupling to the top quark, indicative of physics that lies beyond the currently accepted Standard Model of physics. In summary, our proposed observatory provides a robust platform for searching for new physics and understanding the nature of the Higgs boson's coupling to quarks, particularly through the use of partial widths of Higgs boson decays. This innovative method expands the capabilities of active learning, allowing for more subtle user input, and it can operate independently or in conjunction with existing methods to optimize performance. Our proposed techniques allow for multi-faceted performance assessment, error identification, and model adjustments, using performance-driven hints rather than traditional approaches. The Kiel OntoDialectology platform aims to facilitate research and collection of information on dialects spoken in Germany. To achieve this, the KODI portal will store data about dialects, their speakers, and audio recordings, while the KODI Corpus is an ongoing project that aims to create a standardized, freely available corpus of spoken German. To identify the dialects in audio recordings, a manually created list of German dialect names was used to develop a classification model through the ScikitLearn library. The model was trained on StyleGAN-nata, but gave priority to non-biased outcomes. The trained model was then used for a dialect classification task, setting a new standard with its level of detail, achieving 68% accuracy on unseen data. To optimize performance, the model was trained on two types of text: a shortened version of the German dialect list and a summary of German dialect names, and using two neural architectures, achieving a combination of the two that performed best at identifying Upper German dialects. The full process is documented in a GitHub repository, enabling others to replicate the results. The next step will be refining the model's language understanding, especially to account for variations in speech, while considering ethical aspects of applying neural networks to dialect identification. The full documentation can be found at https://github.com/kiel-nlp/kodi-corpus, and the portal at https://kodi.klwig.de/. 

Note: This research received funding from the KLWIG (Klärungen zur westlichen Region) initiative, a collaboration aimed at documenting German dialects.

Many languages suffer from inconsistent spellings, where a single word can be spelled differently depending on regional dialects, but also consistently spelled with different interpretations. To address these variations, which cannot be resolved by a single algorithm, a dynamic approach known as inverse text standardization is sought after. This study focuses on a particular subset of these variations – known as Canadian French and Quebec French acentizations – to develop and test an inverse standardization system. By combining both data-driven and rule-based techniques with a generator-based model, the system aims to improve its coverage and inclusivity. This paper details our approach to achieving this goal, which involves using a data augmentation technique to expand the training dataset and enhance the model's performance. The results of our experiment are presented along with challenges we encountered and potential future directions. The study showcases that by applying data augmentation, a single inverse standardization model can effectively process both base and acentized forms of French without needing to be tailored. The pre-trained model and associated code can be found on our GitHub repository. The study also highlights and addresses another crucial element of maintaining linguistic integrity in machine learning modeling – recognizing and accounting for linguistic biases. The outcome of our research indicates an important connection between data enhancement and reducing linguistic biases. Moreover, our analysis reveals that under closer scrutiny, even seemingly neutral AI models reveal substantial biases. This study therefore makes a significant contribution to the ongoing discussion on accountability in AI. The impact of data enhancement and bias evaluation on the performance of linguistic models is explored in depth. Additionally, by evaluating our model's output for fairness and performing an under-sampling experiment, we provide a concrete illustration of methods to identify and rectify discrepancies in linguistic AI models. The study therefore offers valuable insights for developers of language models, whose work is fundamental in creating and sustaining trustworthy AI systems. The study ultimately poses a significant question – what exactly constitutes 'fair' in the context of linguistic models? Given the various possible interpretations, the answer is inherently multifaceted. Consequently, this study proposes a framework for evaluating model output quality, comprised of three distinct components, each addressing a specific aspect of the model's performance: data quality, process effectiveness, and algorithmic fairness. The impact of the model's parameters – training data, processing method, and algorithm – on its output is subsequently examined. Interestingly, our research reveals that despite the model's parameters being distinctly different entities, under under-sampling conditions, the effectiveness of the model is surprisingly comparable, suggesting the need for future investigations. The study ultimately concludes by highlighting crucial next steps
