In recent years, Artificial Intelligence has made significant strides in adapting to diverse linguistic patterns and requirements. However, much of the research has primarily focused on mainstream platforms such as PCs and gaming consoles, leaving the assessment of its applicability to other platforms understudied. This study investigates the feasibility of AI on devices such as smartphones and streaming devices. Our primary objective was to analyze the effect of language models and device capabilities on predicting key phrases and further understand how device limitations can be mitigated through model adjustments. Our findings reveal that compact neural networks can accurately analyze text on devices such as smartphones and streaming devices, even those with limited processing power. We further discovered that reducing the sequence length of key phrases can concurrently alleviate memory constraints and promote faster processing on devices with lower capabilities. Lastly, various neural network architectures and optimization techniques have differing impacts on streaming devices, likely due to variations in CPU architecture, which can affect the deployment of such models on these platforms. Our analysis is supported by experimental findings from various IoT gadgets. Our study contributes to the advancement of AI on devices with constraints by providing guidelines for choosing the most suitable language models and hardware for streaming devices, as well as introducing a new neural network architecture, MinimalMax, which can efficiently process low-resource devices at little to no additional memory cost. This research is believed to be the first of its kind to investigate the feasibility of AI on mainstream IoT streaming devices. Our experiments involve a diverse range of devices, including smartphones, streaming devices, set-top boxes, smart TVs, and tablets. Our study was conducted by jointly maintaining these devices with AI researchers, providing unique insights that earlier studies lacked. Our findings have been published in top-tier conferences, including the 2022 IEEE Workshop on Edge AI for the Internet of Musical Things (EiOuoT 2022) and the 2022 ACM Multimedia Web of Objects Conference (WMX 2022). Additionally, a related study on news analysis was presented at the 2022 IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems (ISCAS 2022). In embedded systems, real-time applications often face a complication due to a mixed setup of periodic and aperiodic tasks with varying levels of importance. The real-time nature of such systems demands that periodic tasks with higher importance receive priority over their periodic counterparts with lower importance, and also take precedence over the numerous aperiodic tasks. However, existing operating systems fail to address this mixed importance issue effectively, leading to a significant drawback in terms of timeliness. To address this limitation, this research introduces a new hypervisor called T-Visor, which runs on top of the existing operating system to manage embedded applications with mixed importance and is itself managed by the operating system. Developed with the awareness of hardware virtualization assistance features, T-Visor is designed to enhance its performance in scheduling capabilities, taking full advantage of the hardware support. By integrating the designed soft timer at the hypervisor, T-Visor achieves an accurate and efficient scheduling implementation. The proposed hypervisor is validated on a platform with x86 architecture using a Linux operating system, and its performance is evaluated using the benchmarks Polybench and Cbench. The evaluation demonstrates that T-Visor outperforms the native execution of applications with mixed importance by a significant margin. Furthermore, T-Visor's performance is compared with other hypervisor solutions, including Xen and KVM, and is found to be superior to both alternatives. The investigation also identifies areas for improvement in the hardware support of virtualization, which could further enhance the performance of T-Visor. The performance evaluation is conducted based on real-time metrics, and T-Visor is found to be able to reduce real-time delays by up to 40\% and guarantee at least a five-fold improvement in the number of guaranteed tasks. To ensure the correctness of T-Visor, an extensive evaluation is performed, validating its performance and establishing its reliability through comprehensive analysis, testing, and validation. The research contributes to the field of embedded real-time systems by introducing a new model for managing mixed importance applications, which addresses existing shortcomings in current real-time operating systems, and is supported by experimental results that demonstrate its effectiveness and accuracy. The work presents and promotes the concept of hardware-assisted hypervisor to manage real-time applications with mixed importance, and is found to be beneficial for both research and practice in the field. The integration of the hard timer at the hypervisor is proposed as a useful mechanism for implementing real-time scheduling of applications with mixed importance, and is found to enhance the performance of T-Visor in managing such applications.

In various fields, it is common to encounter both individual and inherited data as well as stochastic processes that are amenable to mathematical analysis. However, the existing theory of stochastic processes focuses primarily on the behavior of individual systems, neglecting the concept of heritability. To address this gap, we propose a framework that integrates both stateful and heritable information, allowing us to evaluate the long-term persistence of endogenous and exogenous traits. Specifically, we demonstrate that the probability of survival for both types of traits decreases exponentially with time when the underlying process is a locally diffusive walk, but this pattern is more complex when the process is locally protective or eroding. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of this framework to phenomena such as viral resistance and the adoption of social movements. By establishing a simple condition for the calculation of long-term survival probabilities, we show that the rates of endogenous and exogenous extinction increase exponentially with time, providing a unified explanation for the phenomenon of social and cultural persistence. To further explore this concept, we conduct an empirical analysis of the adoption of civil rights movements, revealing a striking inverse relationship between the rates of participation and the rates of persecution and prosecution. Our findings serve as a foundation for a broader investigation of the interplay between heritable data and stochastic processes, with potential applications in the fields of genetics, epidemiology, and cultural dynamics. Moreover, we highlight the need for more sophisticated mathematical tools to describe the behavior of systems that integrate both heritable and state-based information, especially in cases where the underlying processes are Markovian. To address this challenge, we outline a novel research agenda, emphasizing the development of heritable stochastic process theory, with an emphasis on the creation of a new framework that is both intuitive and computationally efficient. To facilitate this goal, we invest significant energy in part I of this report, devoting my attention to the development of this theory, supported by an accompanying supplement containing additional illustrations and technical details. In part II of this dissertation, I have the opportunity to engage in a different type of investigation, where I focus on the application of heritable stochastic process to the analysis of data, with a particular emphasis on the exploitation of time-series imaging data to gain insights into the dynamics of inherited systems. In the final section, I present some potential future directions for this research agenda and encourage readers to further develop this topic. Ultimately, I hope that this work serves as a foundation for a new generation of researchers to explore the fascinating intersection of heritable data and stochastic processes. One of the most compelling aspects of quantum mechanics is the phenomenon of Bose-Einstein condensation occurring in highly excited states of a collective of particles. In the field of classical nonlinear optics, nonlinear quantum operators have effectively modeled interactions between light waves and their surroundings. We propose a novel classical-NLO model for a pure Bose-Einstein condensat to describe the macroscopic behavior of a highly excited state in a specific type of quantum system, and to derive a corresponding quantum-NLO model for the same state. Furthermore, we outline a general methodology for deriving a quantum-NLO model from its corresponding classical-NLO version, and we highlight key differences between the two models as well as the benefits of using the quantum-NLO approach. In particular, the quantum-NLO model facilitates a direct connection between its key parameters and essential features of the quantum mechanical Hamiltonian, as well as the formation of coherent macroscopic quasiparticles in extremely excited many-body states. As an important side benefit, the use of the quantum-NLO approach also provides a new perspective on the long-standing issue of zero-point dynamics in systems lacking any initial energy. We demonstrate that, even in the absence of any classical dynamics, the quantum-NLO model still predicts a significant zero-point contribution to the dynamic evolution, and this can be expressed in terms of the quantum mechanical Green's function. In the context of the nonrelativistic Bose-Hubbard model used in our main example, the zero-point contribution turns out to be no less than one tenth of the actual dynamic evolution, and in certain cases it can be as large as ninety percent. In general, the application of the quantum-NLO approach appears to be a highly promising way of investigating many-body dynamics even when the corresponding classical-NLO model produces adequate results. Moreover, the approach also provides a powerful tool for extracting valuable coherent light signal for quantum information processing, as well as the possibility of manipulating zero-point fields through engineered metamaterials and the ability to control the rate of quantum heat transfer in novel devices. In particular regarding our main example, the proposed quantum-NLO model facilitates a direct connection between its key parameters and well-known essential features of the quantum superfluid phase of a highly excited Bose-Einstein condensate, and it also provides important new insights into distinct distinct breakdowns of coherent macroscopic quasiparticles and quantum heat transfer in the case of its thermal mixtures with separate conditations of phase. Ultimately, the proposed quantum-NLO approach provides a powerful tool for deeply exploring quantum phase transitions and many-body dynamics

Deep learning models relying solely on real-valued complex systems are inadequate, as they fail to account for the true nature of many real-world problems. Many real-world problems involve inputs and outputs with multiple complex components, as seen in navigation, the complex dynamics of planetary orbits, and other systems. However, current deep learning models are limited in their ability to apply complex number operations, resulting in a need for special processing techniques to simulate complex inputs and outputs. These workarounds significantly increase the model's parameter count, making them less efficient and more difficult to train. In our study, we investigate the use of complex-valued neural networks that can seamlessly handle complex input-output systems. To this end, we propose a novel approach using complex-valued valuations to extend real-valued deep learning models, allowing them to operate directly on complex systems. By allowing the co-domain of a function to be equivalent across multiple complex dimensions, we can unify the training of real-valued models to address complex-input, complex-output problems, while also easily adapting to problems with real inputs and a single complex output. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on multiple datasets, resulting in improved performance and increased efficiency. Additionally, we emit the contribution regarding the equivalence of the co-domain, arguing that it is equivalent regardless of the chosen fixed co-domain. This concept has far-reaching implications, extending beyond the realm of deep learning and applying to all functions. Moreover, we provide an alternative formulation of the problem using fixed co-domain and show that it can be universally applied, offering a novel perspective on this concept. Moreover, the co-domain equivalence is equivalent to the per-domain equivalence that we previously discussed. Our study is a significant step towards addressing complex problems using deep learning models, representing a major improvement over the current surrogate solutions. We believe that it will have a lasting impact on the field of deep learning and its applications. Furthermore, our implementation has been automatically converted to TF into an TensorFlow model, allowing for easy deployment, as described in the repository.

It is demonstrated that this novel metric embeds multiple established centrality metrics into a single assessment. Due to its computational efficiency, it is suitable for large, complex networks. As an example of its application, Gromov centrality was used to forecast failed nodes within the Facebook transport network.  Lastly, it is discussed how Gromov centrality can be extended to assess the temporary centrality of nodes within time-dependent networks.  Consequently, it has the potential to greatly impact predictive network maintenance technology. We are examining global characteristics of a particular type of dynamical system, which consists of discrete points or intervals along a continuous line. Our focus is on continuous systems where the velocity is always positive, resulting in point trajectories that never repeat and have smooth, monotonic patterns. These systems are particularly challenging to study due to the high dimensionality of their configurations. To analyze their behavior, we use comprehensive global maps, which help identify global patterns and offer a new approach to understanding these complex systems. Our initial application of this method to a particular type of system has allowed us to make significant discoveries about its global patterns, including the existence of universal attractors under specific conditions and the presence of complex, irregular patterns at high velocity values. Our study also provides a framework for classifying system types based on their global patterns and uncovers new types of universal attractors. Although our current analysis is restricted to square-shaped grid structures, which only account for a limited aspect of the system's complete behavior, we are working on developing general tools to help study these systems' global patterns. Our use of global maps has yielded valuable insights into how these systems' behaviors vary based on their complexity and has provided a systematic approach to understanding the system's dynamics. A new quantum algorithm has been developed that adapts to change by using qubit excitements to refine a variational quantum eigensolver's accuracy, thereby reducing its overall cost by utilizing fewer qubit invocations. This adaptive approach first employs a VQE-like algorithm with an initial, lower-specification quantum computer to generate an approximate answer, then uses that result to guide an optimization routine that fine-tunes a more-accurate, higher-specification quantum computer. This optimization is driven by excited qubits, which also help reduce the solver's cost: the higher-specification solver needs only be run for a shorter period and with fewer repetitions. Experimental results demonstrate that the adapted solver outperforms standard ones, achieving up to 90% cost savings, while also providing similar or better outcomes for certain quantum systems, such as the Hartree-Fock solution for carbon dioxide and the ground state of hydrogen fluoride. This algorithm represents a promising option for companies looking to use imperfect, NISQ-era quantum computers effectively in practical applications. One potential extension would be to apply it to more complex quantum systems. While the algorithm was mainly tested on systems with relatively few qubits, its potential has also been demonstrated in multi-qubit systems, where it was found to perform well even at a qubit count of 12. Future research could focus on further developing the algorithm and making it suitable for very large-scale quantum computing applications. The typical learning process in a generative model involves the representation of data. Unlike our conventional approach, where representation learning is tied to recognition models that approximate the inverse of the data distribution, it can be beneficial to relax this inverse mapping to obtain more accurate approximations of intermediate representations. In this study, we show that these intermediate representations are tied to the modes of a specific approximated distribution, known as the profound generative decoder. This new method is founded on an adapted version of a current probabilistic framework and is paired with an updated variational autoencoder framework. Our results demonstrate that these representations are more accurate and provide a greater sense of context. Furthermore, we also explore their applicability in a conditional generative model and reveal the potential of their translation to more robust tasks. The paper introduces a multi-objective branch and bound algorithm that explores the potential of utilizing nested collections of continuous and discrete variables to yield higher quality solution sets.
Initially, a corresponding branch and bound algorithm is formulated for each objective, assuming all variables are either continuous or discrete.
Next, a hybrid approach that combines the analytical bounds of the continuous algorithm with the exploration of discrete search spaces in a non-dominated sampling manner is proposed.
This technique, dubbed MoMBB-NSGAII, utilizes objective upper bounds obtained from the continuous algorithm and projects discrete solutions to a pseudo set of mixed integer non-linear constraints to determine lower bound qualities for each objective.
MoMBB-NSGAII represents a novel addition to the family of multi-objective branch and bound algorithms, distinguished by its ability to efficiently manage large datasets by avoiding the conversion of discrete solutions to lower bound estimations.
Rather, it follows a deep and comprehensive exploration of the dominant front, similar to the NSGAII algorithm, which is particularly suited for computational analysis.
Empirical research demonstrates that MoMBB-NSGAII finds more accurate solution sets compared to generalized branch and bound algorithms. Additionally, it outperforms these algorithms in computational efficiency.
In this research, MoMBB-NSGAII was implemented using the C++ programming language and tested on the well-known multi-objective MISO problem as well as other optimized test problems designed to evaluate algorithm performance and robustness. In this study, we use a synthetic approach based on distribution theory to define and explore linked groupoids and their interactions with manifolds. This work reveals that linked groupoids possess inherent geometric properties and their translation is an exponential map, similar to that of Lie groupoids. Additionally, this research establishes a connection between linked groupoids and Carnot groups, and it expresses principal bundles with their bundle of jets as linked groupoids. This research also demonstrates that linked groupoids can be used to define a generalized version of Lie groups within the context of synthetic differential geometry. Furthermore, it highlights the distinction between linked groupoids and their potential relationships with hyperplane arrangements. Lastly, this research identifies an application of linked groupoids in the field of geometry. More specifically, it shows that the configuration space of a central force field can be constructed as a linked groupoid. If time permits, some additional results and their implications will be discussed. These include implicit function theorems for distributional maps, the expression of momentum maps as distributional logarithms, and their potential applications in geometry and physics. These theorems suggest that distributional geometry may be used to provide geometric interpretations for certain cohomological invariants, such as the symplectic Chern class. They could also potentially be generalized to more complex arrangements of submanifolds in Euclidean space, similar to those defined by hyperplane arrangements but with higher dimensions. If time allows, the possibility of extending this research to the realm of Lie algebroids and their related Poisson structures will be explored. One key finding here would be the potential for blow-ups to be expressed as stacky fibrations, similar to the structure of linked groupoids. Ultimately, this research aims to reveal the rich and far-reaching implications of a simple and fundamental observation concerning the product of two distributions. More specifically, when these distributions are complemented in a suitable sense, their product results in a distinctively new and powerful geometric entity, namely the tangent bundle itself. This seemingly trivial observation has far-reaching implications, not only in geometry, but also in the broader context of synthetic differential geometry. One potential application of these theorems would be the identification of certain distinguished submanifolds within the Arrangement compactification of a manifold. These submanifolds, in turn, could potentially serve as key elements in the broader context of differential geometry. One such submanifolds is the divisor D that arises within the Arrangement compactification of a manifold as a result of duality between a vector bundle and its dual.

A key challenge in developing effective universal parsing models lies in their ability to accurately grasp complex tree structures, which is crucial for informed decision-making as well as translating human language. While prior research focused primarily on syntactic analysis, recent breakthroughs reveal that universal parsing models can achieve high levels of accuracy in terms of part-of-speech identification across various languages. However, these models are hindered from realizing their full potential by subpar performance in universal tree structure extraction. In this study, a novel approach is presented that integrates sequence labeling techniques for tackling the intricacies of universal tree extraction. This innovative method builds upon existing ideas by leveraging a newly conceived syntactic feature extraction approach, which outperforms current standards. Furthermore, a novel mechanism for addressing semantic analysis via universal table extraction is proposed, demonstrating greater feasibility in its application compared to previous attempts. Experimental findings from testing over 40 languages validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Importantly, a major advantage of the proposed model lies in its capacity for cross-linguistic transfer, which is illustrated through application on low-resource languages that were previously understudied. A practical application of the proposed model involves utilizing it in the creation of an online platform for translating text from various languages into English, which shows promising results in maintaining context. The technical specifications and source code of the proposed model are publicly available for further development and use. In particular, the model's performance on tree extraction is notable, achieving 90.44% accuracy, a significant improvement from the current benchmark of 75.81%. This study's findings are expected to pave the way for significant advancements in universal parsing and semantic analysis. A neutron star merger leads to a transient, bright electromagnetic event caused by radiation from viscously heated disks. These disks are initially powered by neutrino cooling, but later by radioactive heating, predicting a distinct pattern where the optical and UV light peaks at different times. However, for extremely low-mass neutron star partners, the disks may not receive enough heating from the resulting stricken object and instead exit powered by neutrino cooling, potentially within days. We examine how strong magnetic fields in this scenario affect the disk using 2D MHD simulations, finding that a magnetic field dominating the disk can either prolong or shorten the period before it transitions to a freely evolving, rotationally driven disk. These simulations also imply a greater optical than UV emission due to the magnetic field's impact on the emission spectrum. We find that for 90% confidence, a postmerger disk must either enter a freely evolving, rotationally driven state within 30 minutes or a magnetically controlled disk within 2.5 days. These results are consistent with early exits in several observed objects, such as PS1-JD539+CFO, Zwicky Transient 2018c, and a few others, in addition to recovering the time-proportional optical-UV luminosity relationship, but not the UV-to-X-ray curvature seen in AT2018cow due to the disk entering the magnetorotator phase. The behavior of AT2018cow still suggests a unique, long-term particle-mediated interaction, possibly involving a protracted low-level gamma-ray burst. These results imply that for very low-mass, double neutron star mergers, the optical-UV luminosity typically decouples just minutes to hours after the explosion, whereas higher-mass systems enter this phase much later, at roughly hours to days. Finally, the expected high-mass fraction of these low-mass, postmerger exits may lead to a significant subclass of low-mass, merger-driven explosions defined by weak, sustained UV emission, where a substantial volume of material is dragged onto a neutron star by magnetohydrodynamic activity. This type of event could be detected at greater distances thanks to the involvement of gravitationally scattered light in the ultraviolet band. In fact, the predicted rate of low-mass, UV-faint explosions is roughly 30-100 times greater than that of bright, kilonovae, and this potential difference in magnitude could be verified by the discovery of low-mass, faint, and long-lived explosions detected by the Roman Space Telescope. The delayed and simultaneous optical emissions from FRBs have the potential to offer a closer look at the burst site. We gather a collection of 22 events where an FRB was accompanied by an optical emission, and a possible connection is found between a particular type of optical burst and the FRB's decay pattern. Furthermore, our study sets limits on the level of optical emission that took place either at the same time or followed the FRB burst.  The constraints we obtained make magnetic field origins less feasible, with a possibility of further research needed, while the opposite effect also presents a challenge, requiring more data and possibly a combination of magnetic fields and plasma effects to better understand these bursts.  The outcome of this study lends good faith to the possibility of observing an FRB origin with the aid of highly advanced and precise optical telescopes like HST or Keck. Recent breakthroughs with large language models have transformed natural language processing tasks, yet many current evaluation methods rely on synthetic, manipulated text, which does not accurately reflect real-world tasks involving direct human-laptop interaction. To bridge this gap, we propose a new set of tasks and evaluation methods that incorporate visual elements to simulate a more authentic, visually-driven approach to text creation. This new framework allows language models to combine textual knowledge with visual information to produce content, demonstrating capabilities that are closer to real-world applications. To implement this idea, we developed iOVA, a web-based platform that integrates visual elements with text creation, accompanied by a comprehensive set of evaluations that scrutinize a language model's capacity to accurately utilize visual signals effectively. iOVA provides a range of intuitive, visually-driven interfaces, allowing both automated and manual configurations to suit various usage scenarios. Importantly, iOVA gives human models the capacity to harness visual data effectively, paving the way for the development of more intelligent, visually-savvy human-computer interactions in the future. When applied to a GPT3 model, our results show that this new approach leads to a significant enhancement in its performance, indicating that visual elements can be efficiently processed and harnessed by large language models. This new evaluation method is expected to offer a fresh, visually-inspired perspective on text creation, ultimately pushing the boundaries of what is considered feasible in natural language processing. To facilitate the broader distribution and utilization of iOVA, all of its associated code and data have been publicly released at https://github.com/NVIDIA-iq/iOVA. By doing so, we aim to foster a new research paradigm that integrates visual elements into natural language processing, ultimately broadening our understanding of what is considered feasible in the field. In contrast to traditional RingCT, our proposed scheme leverages the hierarchical deterministic wallet feature to generate an extended public key set, replacing the random public key set typically used in RingCT. Additionally, our analysis compares the anonymity of transactions involving a single sender and multiple senders, revealing that transactions involving a single sender offer enhanced anonymity. Furthermore, we develop tools to measure the relationship between sender anonymity and the number of extensions in the public key set. Our research also demonstrates that DRingCT can be implemented within present-day infrastructure without necessitating significant upgrades, while offering improved anonymity and transaction verification speed. More specifically, our results indicate that transactions involving a single sender can achieve comparable anonymity to those employing RingCT with 5 or fewer extensions in their public key set. Moreover, our analysis shows that transactions involving multiple senders can attain enhanced anonymity when conducted using 10 or more extensions in their public key set. Notably, we observed an increase of up to 10% in transaction anonymity when utilizing 10 extensions in the public key set. Moreover, our research finds that the value of the 90th percentile of the transaction anonymity index is approximately 7, indicating a significant improvement. Consequently, our research validates the feasibility and effectiveness of DringCT as a suitable solution for Privacy Aware Delegated Proof of Stake. For the LHC's high-luminosity upgrade, an advanced beam monitoring system is being developed to support operator decisions during normal operation, beam adjustment, and diagnosis of issues. An innovative brightness scanning technique is proposed as a key component of the system, enabling fast and precise measurement of beam properties to identify and resolve problems. Although initially, the primary focus is on the PS and SPS, the approach will likely benefit other accelerators as well. We will review various brightness scanning methods, evaluate their effectiveness, and examine the feasibility of implementing the technique in the LHC. Moreover, we will discuss the integration of brightness measurement capabilities into existing beam control systems and consider the potential applications of this technique in the detection of beyond Standard Model physics. An in-depth analysis is performed, taking into account the technique's physics foundations and various experimental aspects such as signal detection, experimental setup, and data interpretation. We review the existing CFA and SCFA methods, assessing their relevance to the proposed technique and identifying their differences and similarities. Moreover, the detection of certain rare exotic physics phenomena, such as e.g. Z', Y, and contact interactions, is discussed and the relevant parameter regions are identified. Finally, the technique is evaluated in the context of existing experiments such as CDF II, LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS, and the importance of precisely measuring beam energies and angularities is recognized. The integration of brightness scanning at the experiment level will likely enhance our understanding of this technique and its applications, and the development of a software package is proposed to facilitate the implementation and evaluation of this technique in experiments and the CDS, the beam monitoring system. The development will be carried out in two stages, with the first focusing on the SPS and PS and the second encompassing the entire LHC. More detailed discussions and evaluations are conducted for each stage, and the feasibility of implementing the technique is assessed. Ultimately, the technique is deemed feasible from both technical and physical perspectives, and the importance of implementing it at the SPS is recognized given the current lack of diagnostic tools. The technique is expected to be available within the next six to seven years, and its development is anticipated to benefit not only the LHC but also other accelerators such as the FAIR as a result of the underlying general principles of beam physics and instrumentation. Recent advances in mathematical modeling have significantly benefited from machine learning and data analysis tools, as researchers can now utilize experimental and clinical data to inform mechanical and biochemical models, thereby optimizing their outcomes and predictions. This research notes that a primary consideration in modeling has been missing from the current literature, which is the essential role of data in informing both the modeling process and the resulting model. This critical aspect of modeling has considerable implications for communicating model results, comparing individual model outcomes, and verifying models via parameter estimation. To address this gap, the study introduces the concept of collaborative data-informed modeling, which is a two-fold approach consisting of data-informed modeling and collaborative learning. This method involves combining and contrasting the outcomes of distinct models, each built using different data types and mathematical formulations, to generate novel insights. To demonstrate the potential of this approach, several case studies are presented, which are rooted in notable scientific inquiries, including understanding speed-based variations in cancer diffusion, detecting anomalies in brain tissue, and modeling systemically administered drug transport within healthy and atherosclerotic vessels. These case studies showcase how combined model analysis can uncover previously unknown biological complexities, such as the interactions between diffusion, tissue type, and location, which may hold the key to explaining how primary aortic diseases contribute to additional cancers. This research promotes the use of data-informed models as a means of advancing our understanding of biological systems and suggests that this approach may lead to breakthroughs in multiple fields, particularly in modeling based on discrete clinical measurements, which has yet to be explored. Ultimately, the study identifies areas for future growth and outlines the expectations for future modeling outcomes, which have the potential to significantly expand our knowledge of biological systems and contribute to groundbreaking discoveries. This paper presents a novel optimization method called AskewSGD to design quantized neural networks efficiently. AskewSGD is a decentralized, iterative optimization technique that achieves this task, outperforming previous methods in terms of computational efficiency. Each iteration of AskewSGD involves two steps: first, it generates a training signal within a specified range based on the current weights, ensuring that the signal's range conforms to the quantization constraints; second, the network parameters are updated using a gradient-based approach. As a result, AskewSGD maintains its robustness even when faced with nonconvex optimization problems and can train complex quantized neural networks efficiently. AskewSGD's reliability is further reinforced by its capacity to train any quantized neural architecture, including those that utilize non-uniform quantization schemes. AskewSGD's performance in terms of maintaining accuracy and reducing training time is comparable to that of Decentralized Gradient Descent, according to theoretical analysis. Through simulation-based evaluation, AskewSGD has been shown to significantly outperform existing techniques, delivering up to a 5x improvement in training time while maintaining accuracy within 1% of the best-performing method. Ultimately, AskewSGD's efficiency has been demonstrated through its successful application in a real-world scenario, namely, the control of nonlinear energy-based neural networks with continuous and quantized inputs. The continuing advancements in soft robotics technology are expected to open up various new applications, making it a highly promising field in the future. A key factor contributing to this optimism is the introduction of machine learning techniques, which have significantly improved predictive models used in planning, leading to more efficient and effective plan execution. In this paper, we examine the application of model driven control in soft robotics and identify areas for improvement. While the predictive accuracy of current models is limited, these models have shown great potential in facilitating more streamlined control systems and controlling complex movements. However, improving model driven control in soft robotics requires the development of more precise predictive models that can learn and adapt to new situations. Current model learning methods primarily rely on real-world data, which may not be sufficient for understanding the underlying physical properties of a system, particularly in non-realistic simulation environments. As a result, integrating model driven control and learning methods remains a major challenge in the field. A potential solution could lie in the use of data generated through physics-informed neural networks. This would allow for the learning of nearly precise predictive models, and consequently, more efficient and effective plan execution. However, this approach also poses several challenges, including the need to separate noise from meaningful data and identifying crucial system parameters. Ultimately, improving model driven control in soft robotics requires a deeper understanding of the physical properties of a system, and while the predictive models may not need to be perfect, they do need to be sufficiently accurate for execution. This study presents an overview of the application of model driven control in soft robotics and identifies specific areas for improvement, including the development of more precise models that can be learned through data and simulation. A key potential solution lies in the use of data generated by physics-informed neural networks, and this work follows on from a previous study outlining the application of model driven control in hard systems. The present study expands on this by exploring model driven control in soft robotics and identifying areas for further research. A accompanying video is available at https://youtu.be/4RrTozY3yOo. The Jacobi group defined by Schottky's formula incorporates all Jacobis, a fact previously recognized except for whether this group is discrete. Although our paper proves the Jacobi group is discrete, this group is properly understood within the context of its inhomogeneous form. Breaking down the group's generators into their corresponding translations and Möbius transformations reveals a clear link between these elements and the action of certain elements on the Riemann surface associated with a genus of at least two. Additionally, our paper provides a novel, concise demonstration of the group's discrete nature. Furthermore, our inhomogeneous representation facilitates a distinct analysis of the group's action on the Riemann surface, a topic we plan to explore in a future publication. Ultimately, our paper demonstrates that the Jacobi group's action on the Riemann surface is properly torsional. We have taken the opportunity to reexamine the Authentic Jacobi Group as part of a larger study of the Authentic PSL(2,R) Group Series, a comprehensive research endeavor focusing on the group's fixed point and periodic points on the Riemann surface. A main objective of this series is to validate Igusa's conjecture, which asserts that the Authentic Jacobi Group, defined by Schottky's formula, is the only Jacobi group that meets the criteria for being generated by elementary transformations and possessing a finitely generated Fuchsian subgroup. The typical fact is presented in a sentence form, but to accurately validate it, additional contextual information is often required, usually provided in a more detailed format, such as a table. This study introduces the table-oriented fact validation disintegration task where the main objective is to break down a fact verification problem into sub-tasks reliant on table components, posing a new set of challenges for existing fact validation models and the fact validation community as a whole. Furthermore, it proposes an improved language model, TONUE, which effectively utilizes numerical table signs to enhance fact validation accuracy, outperforming current standards and confirming the validity of the disintegration hypothesis. The proposed approach and models are supported by experiments, manual evaluations, and an official evaluation challenge launched by the authors. Critical healthcare discoveries, such as new diseases and treatment benefits, often rely on statistical inference methods that help identify substantial changes. However, detecting substantial changes can be challenging especially when working with complex data and limited resources. Recent advancements in statistical modeling have created opportunities to improve out-of-sample detection, a problem encountered when trying to identify when a process has started to deviate from its usual behavior. Building upon existing research by Owen and Oksanen (2020) and Liu et al. (2020), who revisited the field and provided an accurate and efficient model using a Bayesian approach, we have refined the basic behavior model by allowing for varying patterns in the data using a predictive process derived from a distributional Gaussian process. Our new model offers greater flexibility than the original basic behavior model while maintaining out-of-sample performance and is complemented by an exact detection method that is faster and more efficient than the original approach using a predictive process. Moreover, our new model is also the first to allow for the simultaneous detection of multiple beneficial effects in Bayesian inference models, which up until now had only been capable of detecting a single effect. Our new models have been successfully tested on a variety of realistic simulation scenarios and real-world clinical trials where they have proven effective at detecting substantial changes. Finally, the methods in this study have been made available as an easy to use R package that provides a set of tools for performing out-of-sample detection using predictive process Gaussian models. Deep neural networks' success stems from their ability to effectively minimize loss in high-dimensional parameter spaces, but specific loss functions can hinder training by creating local minima that hinder gradient-based optimization.  We examine how various loss functions affect the direction and magnitude of the gradient, particularly in multiclass classification tasks.  We find that the Kullback-Liebler divergence produces an undesirable gradient direction that can impede convergence, while the hinge loss produces an irregular gradient magnitude that can complicate analysis.  We propose a novel modification to the KL divergence that addresses these issues, and demonstrate its efficacy in reducing training time in image classification tasks.  We also provide a systematic method for evaluating the effectiveness of a loss function, quantifying the degree of the gradient's distortion across the entire parameter space.  Our findings have significant implications for the selection of suitable loss functions for specific tasks, potentially leading to optimized model performance.  We validate our observations through comprehensive experiments and analyses, accompanied by an open-source implementation of the proposed methodology.  Our results indicate that the proposed model, trained employing the suggested modified KL divergence, achieves a 60% reduction in the intensity of the gradient's distortion. To enhance the responsiveness of the power grid, a new strategy has been proposed which enables a temporary decrease in voltage at consumer end-devices to minimize losses in the distribution network. This conservative approach, known as ideal CVDA (i-CVDA), aims to improve the controllability of the grid by optimizing voltage at consumer nodes while reducing energy loss and improving the thermal efficiency of network components. Traditional methods for optimizing i-CVDA rely on a central control system but have a key drawback: if the central control system fails, it will be impossible to achieve i-CVDA. To address this limitation, a new distributed i-CVDA algorithm has been developed and demonstrated on the IEEE 33-bus network. This study shows that the stability of the distributed algorithm is guaranteed and provides an analytical proof of convergence, outperforming the centralized approach which fails in certain network configurations. Additionally, the research highlights the importance of forming clusters in the power grid to further reduce energy loss and thermal degradation. This study provides valuable insights which can be used to design more efficient power networks with less energy losses and a greater degree of stability. In connection with the interface conformal field theory, we investigate a reflected entropy proposal. Initially, we focus on a specific scenario involving a conformal interface in a 2-dimensional space, and then extend our analysis to a more complex case involving two separate conformal interfaces. Using a method combining analytic and numerical approaches, we calculate the reflected entropy in both situations. Furthermore, we verify that the numerical contributions to the reflected entropy, originating from the boundary or interface modes, are consistent with the predictions of the holographic dual superconformal gauge theory. Ultimately, we also investigate the relationship between the numerically calculated reflected entropy and the average Hamiltonian density across one of the interfaces. An agreement is found between this value and the reflected entropy in the case of a single conformal interface. For the scenario involving two conformal interfaces, however, we observe a discrepancy and present theoretical arguments to explain this discrepancy. Additionally, we note that the average Hamiltonian density can be regarded as a reflection-free version of the reflected entropy. Similar ideas and results apply to the case of a conformal boundary in a 2-dimensional space, where the role of interfaces is played by the Cardy-like boundary modes. As in the previous scenario, our calculations of the reflected entropy involving these modes are consistent with the predictions of the AdS/BCFT correspondence, and once more, we observe a disagreement between the reflected entropy and the average Hamiltonian density in the case of a conformal boundary. An explanation for this disagreement is provided. Moreover, we speculate that the difference between the reflected entropy and the average Hamiltonian density could serve as a distinct indicator of the presence of a boundary or interface in a 2-dimensional space. An accompanying movie is provided, containing the data necessary to validate the numerical results presented in this study. This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems. The tool is built upon a traditional subset of C and is intended to facilitate the creation of ACL2 proofs for existing C code by translating it into a form that can be proven within ACL2. This research presents VACA, a Python package created to build and test variational graph autoencoders for causal modeling purposes. We explain the key components of VACA, including its implementation of three influential models (Kumon et al., 2020, Odening et al., 2020, Long et al., 2020) that use observational data to make predictions about causal relationships. In addition to these implementations, which are based on existing ideas, VACA includes original modifications to one of the models to improve its performance when dealing with scenarios involving synthetic data. VACA's results are compared with those generated by causal inference tools, with the aim of establishing its effectiveness in making predictions about causal relationships. The Irish LOFAR facility serves as the northernmost component of the LOFAR network, capable of collecting data from up to 27 individual stations, covering an extensive area of around 1000 square degrees. REALTA is an innovative beamformed LOFAR capture system based in the north of Ireland, continuously processing data in near real-time to facilitate the analysis of transient radio signals. This system has generated a substantial database of 343 million hours of recordings across 244 frequency channels from January to December 2021, spanning an enormous 27x27 degree region. During the capture period, REALTA identified a wide range of persistent point sources, radio frequency interference (RFI) features, and solar system objects. It also collected data on pulsars, quasars, and provided improved coordinates for known sources such as the Crab pulsar and the Cas A supernova remnant. Furthermore, REALTA's data included 2985 rotationally modulated planetary sources, with notable examples being the Venus 2.3 day amplitude variable, the Earth at 1 Hz, and the Saturn Mimas 40-day modulation. Finally, REALTA's archives contain 20,062 fast radio bursts (FRBs), demonstrating a high level of efficiency in detecting these elusive signals and paving the way for future projects. Future projects will involve processing data in an even more timely manner, expanding the scope to the entire LOFAR network and leveraging state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms to streamline the detection of interesting radio transient phenomena.

By manipulating light at a molecular or atomic level, a vast array of untapped materials becomes accessible. This opens doors to innovative technologies in sensing, healthcare, and environmental monitoring, among others. To bring metaphotonics to the forefront, developers must perfect their designs, but the complex interaction of light with matter creates hurdles in optimizing metaphotonic devices. To overcome these challenges, researchers are turning to artificial intelligence, which holds great promise for refining metaphotonic designs. This article will detail the fundamentals of metaphotonics, highlighting the pivotal role that AI must play in its pursuit. Furthermore, researchers will present some of the existing AI-driven methods for developing metaphotonic devices and introduce the "Clever Metaphotonics by AI" (CMA) framework. This framework, designed to tackle the complexities of metaphotonic device development, includes two main components. Our research focuses on cross-language information retrieval using images, where we are given an image and two text domains, and we aim to find relevant images across languages. To this end, we developed a hybrid framework that combines interactive and non-interactive approaches to leverage the strengths of each. The framework involves first using pre-trained image features and a cross-lingual text-image distance metric to generate initial candidate images through vector subtraction, and then refining these candidates interactively with a user, or simply ranking them without user involvement. Our experimental results show that the hybrid framework enables accurate and efficient cross-language image retrieval and demonstrate that its performance can be further enhanced by incorporating various enhancements, such as duplicate candidate filtering and pre-training on multilingual datasets. Moreover, our analysis reveals that our framework's performance can be interpreted as a combination of two key factors: (i) the accuracy of its initial non-interactive ranking, which identifies promising candidate images, and (ii) the effectiveness of its interactive refinement process, which verifies the relevance of those candidates through user involvement. Notably, our research sheds light on the benefits of integrating interactive and non-interactive techniques for a more comprehensive understanding of multilingual image-based information retrieval. The source code for our framework is now publicly available to foster further research in this area, and our results suggest that the key to future success lies in jointly designing interactive and non-interactive methods that capitalize on their complementary strengths. The proposed approach has promising implications and could likely be adapted for other related tasks, such as zero-shot learning, where the goal is to achieve successful learning without any need for user annotation or involvement. And interestingly, our research reveals that the combination of interactive and non-interactive methods exhibits surprising parallels with the long-standing query-by-image paradigm in the field of information retrieval. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the roles and complexities involved in designing effective interactive and non-interactive retrieval frameworks, and highlight potential strategies for harnessing their benefits. The source code for our framework is now publicly available at https://github.com/ameer-kayser/clicir.

When conducting surveys in large countries with diverse regions, surveys often face the challenge of achieving sufficient sample sizes for accurate interpretation. Region-specific analysis faces a different challenge, namely achieving representation beyond their own borders. This paper discusses two distinct strategies for addressing these challenges: expanding sample sizes and conducting sub-national analyses. It explores the advantages of these strategies, their limitations, and suggests potential solutions. The presentation is based on an analysis of a low-income country's recent demographic and health survey. The research found notable variations in some key indicators between sub-national regions, and it suggests that targeted small-region estimations could be an effective way to enhance sub-national analysis, even with limited sample sizes. Additionally, it recommends a more extensive implementation of small-region estimations, and it outlines model-based estimation techniques that can be used to generate reliable estimates for small regions. The recommendations include increasing the minimum threshold for meaningful small-region estimations, and implementing comprehensive small-region models that leverage regional key variables to produce confident estimates. The techniques proposed in this study are now available for practical application. The presentation concludes by highlighting important areas of research related to small-region models.

The transformation of a prestellar core into a planetary disk is investigated through a series of simulations, starting with free-expanding disks that mimic the prestellar core's structure and the surrounding environment. Two variations of the disk's initial properties were examined: one with a steep density gradient and another with near-isothermal properties. When the disk's accretion rate and steep density gradient are high, the free-expanding disk ruptures and develops a compact, wide planetary disk. This planetary disk then rapidly grows in mass due to accretion, shrinks in radius due to photoevaporation, and develops a unique structure with a short outer dust layer. In contrast, when the disk's initial properties are near-isothermal, the rupture results in a smaller planetary disk with a larger radius. These simulations suggest that planetary disks can form through the rupture of prestellar cores, and potential observations of these disks can provide insight into the formation process. Further research is required to develop a comprehensive model of disk formation and development. A related movie is available at https://dx.doi.org/10.26073/2021ujzf5j/1. This paper presents our findings from a campaign to measure the effects of atmospheric activity on laser signals, focusing on the relationships between the auto-correlation of signal fluctuations, the auto-power of these fluctuations, and the corresponding beam size. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the effects of atmospheric turbulence and offers a framework for interpreting observations of various lengths. Importantly, it enables the removal of time-invariant biases inherent in traditional models of the phenomenon. As an alternative, we propose and evaluate a new model that more accurately reflects the natural variability of the atmosphere. This research is essential for analyzing data from different observation periods and, ultimately, for evaluating the effects of atmospheric activity on laser signals in real-time. As an added benefit, we investigate the potential of our model to inform observations of varying lengths, including a discussion of the implications for simulations of the phenomenon for different observation durations. Several data stream mining approaches have been developed to effectively process and analyze high-speed, ever-changing temporal sequences.  Despite their ability to modeled detailed data patterns,  many of these approaches are hindered by several limitations, including the need for enormous amounts of memory and the inability to accommodate variable lengths. Furthermore, the use of high-dimensional models often results in computationally expensive training processes. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel, efficient learning technique that handles multi-term temporal data sequences. This approach leverages a hierarchical prior distribution that enables principled dimension reduction, sparsity, and variable-order modeling. By incorporating observation noise, we model the data precisely and obtain accurate posterior distributions for the parameters. Experimental results on both artificial and real-world data confirm the superiority of our approach compared to established state-of-the-art methods in terms of prediction performance, model size, and computational efficiency. This research is accompanied by an open-source library written in Python, the MTSBSN package, which is freely accessible on GitHub. The paper also includes a demonstration of the MTSBSN library's functionality through an associated Jupyter Notebook. The implementation can be viewed online via GitHub or jupyter.com. The paper concludes by discussing the practical applications of MTSBSN in the context of its substantial memory requirements. Nonetheless, the advent of distributed and cloud-based computing allows for the seamless deployment of MTSBSN on large-scale data. Therefore, MTSBSN's performance and accuracy make it a viable option for real-time systems. The objective of this study is to provide a comprehensive, detailed explanation of Pontryagin duality, going beyond the conventional approach by adopting a continuous reasoning methodology. This enhanced methodology yields not only refined demonstrations but also novel, significant results. In particular, this technique enables demonstration of the continuous duals of certain 'large' topological groups, which had previously eluded discovery. Moreover, this methodology facilitates an intuitive understanding of the complex and often mysterious topological properties of the Pontryagin duals of 'large' groups, which had previously been outside the reach of practical analysis. In addition to these advancements, the introduction of continuous reasoning significantly broadens the scope of applicable reasoning methods in topological group theory, ultimately leading to the derivation of a formalized, continuous proof of the Navier-Stokes equations for arbitrary 3-dimensional manifolds, a requirement of utmost importance for solving the 3-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations. In addition, the methodology is applied to the continuous duals of certain 'large' groups, which had not been previously described in the literature. In particular, the context of locally convex Hausdorff groups, the powers of the rational numbers, and the Prüfer groups play a crucial role in achieving a comprehensive description of the Pontryagin duals of 'large' groups through the application of continuous reasoning. Consequently, the findings presented in this study unify, generalize, and provide a fresh perspective on a diverse range of previously discovered results, which are built upon a combination of the continuous reasoning methodology and the application of powers to 'large' groups. Ultimately, the discovery of a formalized, continuous proof of the Navier-Stokes equations for arbitrary 3-dimensional manifolds represents a significant challenge in the field, which remains incomplete at the time of this current (march 2021) writing. Nevertheless, the advancement of computer vision technology poses significant data privacy risks, making it challenging to utilize intricate human judgments that could lead to biased outcomes. To address these concerns, we must develop a data encryption method that protects participants while allowing for the learning and evaluation processes to be as transparent as possible. Our proposed approach achieves this by reaching a delicate balance between safeguarding the data and maintaining open communication with the judge, thereby ensuring that the learning outcome remains consistent. Our algorithm allows for the training of highly accurate models with justice applications, while demonstrating the importance of differential confidentiality in achieving fair and just results. Moreover, our research showcases the effectiveness of this method on real-world justice applications, as well as highlighting its benefits in low-resource settings where the aggregation of data is a significant challenge. In this research, a method for controlling complex systems based on data is proposed, allowing for direct correction of unrealistic simulations when new information becomes available. This approach applies to systems of any size and includes methods to evaluate the system's state and make decisions in real-time. Our proposed method is practiced on a simulated aircraft to demonstrate its effectiveness, where a learned control strategy is successfully fine-tuned using only a single actual flight with the aid of a flight stability augmentation system. This modification also enabled the system to operate safely without any interventions for an extended period of time. This research demonstrates a major breakthrough in controlling complex systems with limited data and information by achieving successful results on a real-world system for the first time ever, paving the way for similar applications in various complex control problems. As image-capturing technologies become increasingly accessible, the need to develop efficient image-capturing systems has grown in importance. These systems can exploit the natural environment to create novel, high-quality images from a given dataset. In contrast to generative adversarial networks, connection networks offer the advantage of pairing new images with relevant sensory inputs. However, existing image-capturing systems typically lack the capability to ensure consistency between new and existing images, resulting in a classification error when presented with novel scenes. To address this limitation, this study proposes a new framework known as relation GAN, which incorporates triplet loss to establish a more robust and generalizable image-capturing system. Evaluation of the proposed framework on the NUS-WELCOME dataset demonstrates significant improvements, with accuracy rates of 84.65% and 83.58% for the wild and indoor datasets, respectively, surpassing the best existing performance by a substantial margin. These results suggest the efficacy of the proposed system as a highly effective image-capturing solution. A novel TF-QKE system is proposed, utilizing entangled quantum fields across separate optical spectra to facilitate encryption. This approach leverages light partitioning to decode messages, eliminating the need for intense beam splitting and phase synchronization. Instead, the TF-QKE process occurs through the detection of stored quantum states using phase-sensitive amplifiers, which also serve as trusted intermediate stations. Due to the inherent stability of the splitting process, these stations can easily synchronize with both communicating parties, promoting the expansion of the TF-QKE network. Furthermore, our scheme features enhanced security through the use of two-phase encoding, where the first phase encodes the secret key and the second phase ensures security by revealing the original key state, making it highly resistant to attacks. Our scheme exhibits superior performance using phase-encoded polarization states, where the quantum fields' distinct properties alleviate the need for beam splitting, thereby reducing noise during the detection process. Consequently, our TF-QKE system displays great promise for secure communication over long distances utilizing conventional telecommunication systems. Moreover, our analysis shows that our TF-QKE system can withstand both passive and active attacks, with the probability of a secure key being shared being close to 100% for distances below 200 km. This shared security characteristic inherently defends against eavesdropping, thus further enhancing the stability of the TF-QKE process. Although linear loss along the transmission path may slightly reduce the probability of a secure key, this loss can be transferred to the attacker, effectively rendering the benefit of the TF-QKE system to be the shared secret key, which is not affected by linear loss. Consequently, our TF-QKE system can ensure nearly 100% shared secrecy, which is unmatched in traditional QKE systems. Neural architecture search has effectively utilized random search to handle the exploration problem, but its application is limited due to the high computational cost. The disruption theory suggests that tenacious local optimization can arise from this approach. We studied the impact of this phenomenon on NAS through the creation of a simple one-dimensional case study and found that the non-stationary objective function of NAS exhibits hallmark signs of abrupt shift, such as abruptness, irreversibility, and residual disruption that persists even after thorough optimization. In response, we have proposed Skip-AST, an enhanced NAS method that effectively mitigates this phenomenon by skipping over the deep local valleys in a valley hierarchy. Our research is based on a valley-free sample selection strategy and accompanied by a novel sampling method. When evaluated against five benchmark datasets, Skip-AST has shown superior performance compared to state-of-the-art low-cost NAS methods, achieving a notable reduction in inference accuracy discrepancy from 4.44% to 2.24%. Key benefits of time series analysis for real-world applications include: accurately forecasting future data by identifying ongoing trends; understanding past occurrences such as events and their durations; extracting meaningful data from large datasets to analyze patterns; analyzing system downtime and efficiency metrics for overall improvement; examining data related to user behavior like clicks and purchases; and identifying trends in user engagement metrics to boost user experience.  This guide focuses on providing an introduction to the theoretical foundations of time series analysis and presenting an in-depth exploration of the theft package, a comprehensive R library offering an extensive set of tools to conduct sophisticated, attribute-based time series analysis.  Specifically, theft offers time series distortion analysis, comprehensive anomaly detection, and distortion detection with automatic optimal distortion identification.  This paper, written for time series experts and those new to the field, will detail both theoretical and practical uses of distortion analysis and one-point-at-a-time (OPAT) anomaly detection, including practical applications and the precise methods which the theft package employs to achieve these goals. Our research aims to explore the interplay between size and model performance, investigating the merits of smaller models that might achieve similar results as their larger counterparts. We employ trimmable neural network architectures where the model's properties can be modified after training, assessing the effect of trimming on the performance of convolutional networks with varying sizes. Our experiments reveal that even larger convolutional networks may not surpass comparable, fully connected models in specific classification tasks, such as identifying structured patterns, but deliver superior results when handling more complex and nuanced tasks, such as handwritten character recognition. Our analysis stresses the importance of tailoring model designs to specific types of data, and suggests that a more efficient, lottery ticket-like, fully connected model may be the better choice for handling hand-written image classification. Moreover, the inherent properties embedded within convolutional networks make them the superior choice for analyzing and understanding task-specific patterns, as confirmed by evaluating the trimmable architecture's performance using both mutual information and information by position measurement. Finally, our analysis demonstrates that a combination of both approaches, the combination of a pre-trained convolutional network with a separately trained, fully connected model, able to trim the convolutional network's unnecessary attributes, results in the most accurate hand-written digit classification. Our code for the studies has been made publicly accessible at https://github.com/AlGoyal/Neural-Networks-Trimming. What's more, our implementation of the trimmable architecture has the potential to be applied to a broad array of tasks, as revealed by our results in the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, indicating promising outcomes in the future use of the trimmable architecture in the field of image classification. One such promising outcome is the discovery of a trimmable lottery ticket like pattern within the well known ResNet 50 architecture, the outcome of which has the potential to change the way we approach model pruning in the near future. This strategy focuses solely on maximizing ticket accuracy but fails to consider the value of having such a ticket, especially in contexts where the cost of training it might be too high. In response, we've developed a framework for optimizing the anticipated value of a ticket, which takes into account both its accuracy and the model's distance from its pristine state. This framework allows for simultaneous ticket training through the optimization of marketing and purchase decisions. Our experimental results demonstrate the benefits of our proposed approach that balances ticket quality and the cost of training. In addition, we've found that the model's distance can serve as an effective measure of ticket transferability and revealed a critical threshold for achieving highly transferable tickets. Our code is available for review at https://github.com/moebiusduncan/Ticket-Marketing-and-Purchase. With further research, we believe the training cost could be a valuable model selection criterion in the future. Our study also highlights several marketing strategies that enhance ticket performance, especially those involving distillation at minimal cost. While our theoretical model assumes Marketing and Purchase are complementary actions, in practice, we've shown that concurrent execution yields better outcomes than sequential execution. Moreover, we've explained why the ticket training paradigm has not yet been successfully reversed -- that is, optimizing the strongest subnetwork within the best-fitting model rather than the clean model. Our study identifies the reasons behind this phenomenon and provides guidance on the appropriate model structure. Our research also confirms that natural lottery ticket hypotheses exist in practice, and by uncovering their characteristics, we have a better understanding of how to design experiments that generate these hypotheses. Finally, we propose that the problem of optimizing lottery ticket quality is a resolution search challenge, and our theoretical framework is a effective strategy for achieving valuable tickets through the transformation of poorly performing models. Though our theoretical model predates the breakthrough finding that natural subnetworks are relatively resistant to the application of dropout, our results are still relevant in the dropout setting. We've conducted in-depth calculations using diagrammatic Monte Carlo to examine the characteristics of a Fermi polaron in a specific context where particles can move freely in two dimensions. We've developed a technique that allows for the creation of multiple classification models and automatically detects potential biases within each model. Our approach builds upon established theories, incorporating both formal concept analysis and Dempster-Shafer theory, to develop a comprehensive framework. This framework encompasses three key components:  the creation of classification models through the adaptation of available data; the identification of potential biases within these models; and an evaluation of the models' reliability by comparing their results with a unified reference model. From a functional perspective, this study analyzes the integration of postural and movement control systems in a monopod's single bound. Utilizing a muscle-driven simulator based on a simplified model, we examined various parameters including plantar flexibility, foot geometry, and muscle physiology to analyze their impact on single-bounce gaits. By manipulating these factors, we discovered that even minimal changes in these parameters can produce notable alterations in movement patterns. In particular, increased plantar flexibility significantly affects the longitudinal balance of the leaping animal, whereas a larger sole provides additional stability against the pitch resulting from single-bounce impacts. Additionally, we found that slight adjustments in sole flexility or foot shape can produce analogous effects on single-bounce gaits. In terms of muscle physiology, we focused on the function of soleabductor muscles in maintaining lateral balance during single-bounce movements. Our research indicates that a sufficient response of soleabductors to single-bounce impacts is crucial for maintaining balance, whereas a delayed response can increase the risk of pitch during single-bounce movements. In summary, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of single-bounce gaits, taking into account the dynamic interactions between a monopod's control systems, body structure, and muscle physiology. This research also opens up new avenues of investigation on the potential benefits of postural skills in enhancing one-bounce locomotion efficiency. In particular, by employing postural control at the onset of one-bounce preparation, a monopod can achieve a more stable and efficient bouncy gait characterized by increased balance, reduced impact penalties, and more efficient energy usage. Moreover, our study demonstrates that a pre-bounce postural skill allows a monopod to adapt its single-bounce control strategies to accommodate changes in its mechanical structure and muscle physiology, thereby ensuring consistent locomotion efficiency across various body configurations and muscle compositions. In conclusion, our proposed theoretical framework, along with an understanding of single-bounce gaits and postural skills, provides a crucial foundation for designing advanced monopod gaits and understanding the principles of tetrapod locomotion. Potentially, this knowledge could benefit the development of robots and machines capable of stable and efficient single-bounce movements. The majority of IoT devices nowadays boast software-based functionality, and software upgrades are now an essential part of both industrial and residential life. However, these upgrades are prone to errors, particularly in the field, and can have devastating consequences if failed. To mitigate this risk, network architects now employ robust failure handling mechanisms in software upgrades. Nonetheless, a clear definition of network reliability during upgrades remains elusive, and existing literature often rely on implicit definitions or unverified simulations, leaving a gap in knowledge on this topic. To address this limitation, this study conducts a comprehensive real-world evaluation of mesh network resilience in software upgrades through an extensive-scale test involving over 75 IoT devices and multiple hardware platforms. To complement this investigation, a novel reliability metric has been created for extensive-scale evaluations, enabling accurate comparison with simulations and field trials. The results of this evaluation revealed a discrepancy between the observed and predicted reliability values, underscoring the need to refine current failure handling strategies and leading to derivation of best practice guidelines based on real-world evidence. The outcomes and insights from this study will enable researchers and practitioners to better comprehend and tackle software upgrades in large-scale IoT settings, ultimately contributing to developing more reliable IoT applications. The software solution developed in this study is publicly available on GitHub, facilitating future investigations and extensions.
