It then presents a formal semantics for GATT models and defines the Timed Forward Chain Planner as a function based on $\lambda_t$-calculus. The paper establishes and proves three key results: the equivalence of TFCP's termination with the relative realizability of a certain type, the relation of GATT models to this type, and ultimately, the validity of TFCP in generating feasible solutions. The development employs the Relational Model Checker in Haskell for proof assistance. The paper's central contribution lies in providing a formal proof of TFCP's validity, surpassing existing efforts towards validation. The provided semantics serves as a foundation for future rigorous validation and verification of planning algorithms and models. Validation Results

1. TFCP terminates.
2. The model possesses at least one reachable marking.
3. Each world in an optimal plan starts in a marked state.
4. Each world in an optimal plan is marked at its final state.
5. Each optimal world begins and ends in a marked state.

These validation results correspond to key properties of temporal planning, indicating that any plan generated by the Timed Forward Chain Planner is feasible. The provided Haskell code can automatically prove these validation results for any given GATT model.

Current evaluation metrics for summarization tasks have their limitations. Existing guidelines do not thoroughly consider the varied goals of summarization, leading to summaries that may not conform to expected standards. To address this issue, a new assessment metric called SummScore has been proposed. This innovative metric relies on a cross-encoder to accurately establish a connection between human-written summaries and their corresponding articles, effectively gauging summaries based on their ability to retain original information while filtering out redundant content. Unlike conventional evaluation metrics, SummScore assesses summaries in a nuanced manner that considers their structural and textual similarities with the original articles. Furthermore, SummScore is not restricted by the inherent biases of previous evaluation methods. To validate its effectiveness, SummScore was tested on the task of generating news summaries in two distinct categories, long and short summaries. When tested, SummScore demonstrated a more robust capability to distinguish high-quality summaries from low-quality ones, with results showing a more significant correlation with human evaluations. Consequently, SummScore opens up new possibilities for a more standardized evaluation framework for summarization tasks and its accompanying datasets. To facilitate its adoption, the associated code and datasets are publicly available on the SummScore GitHub page at https://github.com/ConfGen/SummScore. Additionally, a corresponding demo page at https://summ-score.com/ allows users to input any summary for evaluation. These resources offer opportunities for developers to test the efficacy of SummScore and explore its potential in creating improved automatic summarization tools. Overall, SummScore holds promise as a groundbreaking evaluation metric, and its success may extend to other text generation areas as well. Finally, further research is needed to encompass a broader range of summarization goals and create an even more comprehensive evaluation framework.

The development of autonomous vehicles relies heavily on a unified sensor integration technique that merges the benefits of 3D LiDARs and cameras while minimizing their limitations. To address this, researchers have been exploring various approaches to combine these sensors, although a reliable and robust technique remains to be fully implemented. This paper presents a novel LiDAR-camera integration framework called BEVFusion that coordinates beam and voxel-based data to benefit from the unique strengths of both devices. By representing LiDAR data as beams and capturing camera information as 2D pixels with depth information, BEVFusion enables the fusion of LiDAR and camera data in a beam-based pixel map. This framework combines the processing of LiDAR and camera data into a unified beam-based system, facilitating the creation of versatile and adaptable detection models. Our experiments show that BEVFusion achieves a good balance between detection accuracy and efficiency, with a notable ability to robustly operate under various sensor resolution conditions. Furthermore, our results indicate that BEVFusion outperforms existing methods, particularly in scenarios with limited camera field of view and low LiDAR resolution. This framework is published under an extremely permissive open-source license to enable researchers and engineers to utilize and build upon its concepts. The code for BEVFusion is made available on our repository at https://github.com/ADLab-AutoDrive/BEVFusion. This research received support from the Honda Research Institute Europe for funding and resources. A comprehensive paper on this work can be found at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.12221.pdf.

High-speed data streams, arriving in near-real-time and often exceeding our processing capabilities, can be handled with streaming computing frameworks, allowing for immediate analysis. Though widely used, current systems have limitations, such as increased processing delay as analysis complexity increases, which is prohibitive for certain scenarios. Our framework improves streaming analytics by offering compact storage and optimized processing times, with the added benefit of enabling complex operations that traditional streaming computing frameworks can't support. In information retrieval related to images, a common issue involves recovering the complete image when only a portion is available or damaged. This problem arises in various fields, including medical imaging, astronomy, and machine vision. When processing image data in a streaming manner, tensor completion methods can efficiently recover the missing information. However, these methods typically require a complete knowledge of the image structure, which is often impractical. To overcome this limitation, techniques like tensor ring and tensor completion utilizing tensor rings have been applied. These methods decompose complex images into a finite number of tensor components and recover the image based on a small set of observed tensor entries. However, they are often plagued by noisy data, biased tensor observation, and incomplete image information. To address these limitations, a new method called patch monitoring-based streaming tensor ring restoration (PM-STR) has been proposed for information retrieval of visual data. This method utilizes a patch-level monitoring mechanism to adaptively correct tensor ring parameters during the recovery process. Furthermore, it employs a local clean sample projection mechanism to refine the patch-level tensor ring parameter update and ensures the minimization of errors. By incorporating a joint optimization of tensor ring parameters and clean sample projection, PM-STR achieves accurate recovery of damaged images under various conditions. To validate its effectiveness, a series of experiments have been conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets to demonstrate PM-STR's superior performance in comparison to other state-of-the-art methods. Using the Streda-Woodruff relation, we investigate the change in the thermodynamic properties of monolayer graphene following an electric charge transition, observed as a shift in the Fermi level from the Dirac point to conic bands. By applying thermodynamic equations, including internal energy, heat capacity, and entropy, we evaluate the effects of this transition. Notably, all these properties exhibit discrete jumps at the transition point and become continuous functions below it. With the inclusion of a non-zero temperature, the electric adjustment of the graphene state displays distinct thermodynamic behavior at the transition point, characterized by discrete changes in its features. These findings demonstrate that the electrically adjusted monolayer graphene exhibits typical three-band characteristics as evidenced by its three-band Eilenberger function and the resulting three-band effective mass. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the heat capacity and magnetization display even/odd parity with respect to the temperature, while the internal energy and entropy display integer-fraction parity. These unique parity relations with temperature distinguish electrically adjusted monolayer graphene from other two-band and three-band materials, such as superconductors, various semimetallic compounds like WTe$_2$, and HgV$_2$O$_5$, where the parity is either absent or only even. Our study focuses on thermodynamic properties at various integer and fractional filling numbers and demonstrates that these can be recovered by applying gauge-invariant Fermi level and its first derivative. These recovery criteria also explain why the electrically adjusted monolayer graphene exhibits integer fill number even parity in a narrow temperature range. Our research provides a foundation to experimentally verify the electrically adjusted monalayer graphene characteristics using specific heat and magnetization measurements that demonstrate integer-fraction parity with temperature. These experiments can also distinguish between electrically adjusted monolayer graphene and other materials with unique thermodynamic properties. Our study further extends by exploring changes in its thermodynamic characteristics after undergoing a superconducting transition. A newly observed period of 12 years has shown that the active star CR Draconis is also involved in a similar interaction.  This period was identified through data collected from the Ooty telescope, as well as an earlier observation from 1999, both of which showed that CR Draconis emits a distinct and stable low-frequency signal during specific times of its rotational cycle.  Researchers discovered that this stability is due to the star's permanent interaction with its companion, as opposed to the typical thermal radio emission associated with active stars which shows greater variability.  The observed radio emission lasts for a long time and has characteristics of electron-cyclotron maser radiation, as well as displaying a distinct anti-correlation with CR Draconis's X-ray levels, suggesting that the radiation originates from a region that is not directly influenced by the star's atmosphere. Our study presents a computational analysis using the lattice cluster algorithm to examine the ground state properties of 2D frustrated quantum antiferromagnets composed of loosely connected three-spin clusters. The findings from simulations of square and triangular lattice structures reveal similarities in their phase diagrams under increased intercluster coupling. The simulations indicate that the existing experimental observations of spin-1/2 antiferromagnetic compounds can be explained by the transition from the extensively researched triimer model to a more realistic weakly-linked model. The use of the lattice cluster algorithm allows for accurate computations of observables in the weakly-linked model for the first time. The applications of our approach are exemplified through investigations of real-world materials such as CsBaCoO3 and Pb3NiTe5. The calculations predict a dimerized state in a layered network of square lattices, as well as an interlaced spin liquid in a triangular lattice structure. The methods employed and findings are further discussed with reference to existing experimental data and theoretical models for quantum frustrated materials. The research highlights potential applications of the lattice cluster algorithm in the investigation of ground state properties and phase transitions in quantum antiferromagnets and other closely-related systems. Recent breakthroughs in large pre-trained language models (PLMs) have led to remarkable advancements in text analysis and generation, also encompassing educational settings. However, the utilization of PLMs in zero-shot education still poses several hurdles, primarily stemming from the difficulty in accurately grasping the inquiry conveyed via a prompt, particularly when it contains further specifications. This study seeks to mitigate these limitations by proposing the concept of Dataset and Prompt Assemblages, wherein a training set comprises multiple datasets, and each instance within these datasets is met with a variety of prompts. This concept allows for the discovery of general, adaptable knowledge in zero-shot education, also providing the capacity to address unfamiliar queries that may not be present in the initial training data. Our framework, known as PATA, is a PLM fine-tuning method that is capable of optimizing both the dataset and prompt asymptotically. Our empirical analysis evaluating the comprehension of complex conceptual inquiries in zero-shot education reveals that PATA is capable of significantly enhancing performance in terms of both overall accuracy and naturalness of responses. Our research further demonstrates that PATA is effective in addressing unfamiliar queries as well as in preventing knowledge poisoning. Lastly, our investigation of PATA's ability to assemble prompts reveals novel and accurate interpretations, and an evaluation of its semantic coherence and rationality indicates that PATA-generated responses are highly coherent and rational. An examination of the PATA-generated answers and prompts, as well as the entailed knowledge, is presented in a Comprehension Report that serves as a distillation of the model's understanding. Our work is dispensed into three parts, comprising a Teacher's Guide, a Research Document, and a Technical Report, providing an in-depth analysis of PATA, including its design, assemblage, and metanalysis. The Teacher's Guide offers an introductory overview utilizing the first seven chapters of the SNAIL dataset and includes elaborate examples, whereas the Research Document presents the full PATA framework utilizing all 428 datasets and includes an exclusive chapter on the theoretical background of Dataset and Prompt Assemblages. Our Technical Report is a detailed description of the PATA implementation, including the Design Theory. Snail is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/jfjia/snail. An initial release of the Dataset and Prompt Assemblages, including 428 datasets and 428K prompts, is freely accessible via https://data.world/jfjia/snail. Natural Language Processing efforts to grasp the meaning of words and sentences intellectually have been advancing rapidly. Nonetheless, current approaches treat language as a mere collection of data to be analyzed; they lack a broader philosophical understanding of language's purpose. Consequently, they are unable to replicate humans' sustained reasoning about language. To fill this theoretical void, semantic interpreters are being developed that factor in prior knowledge along with the analyzed text. Although promising, these interpreters have not yet been applied to any significant real-world challenges due to limitations in their capacity for detailed reasoning, which they achieve through intricate neural networks that require substantial computational resources. Moreover, they have been trained on extensive data sets that reflect a narrow perspective. To break through these barriers, innovative methods are being developed that incorporate human explanations and allow the incorporation of noisy, user-generated content to facilitate understanding, as well as systems that mimic human-like language usage to aid in language mastery. These novel approaches are being successfully tested in intricate, real-world scenarios involving significant computational requirements. Importantly, they have been successfully applied to a variety of unusual input formats, such as three-dimensional animations and the internal workings of computer systems, highlighting the significance of theoretical language analysis in the development of cutting-edge AI technologies. It is the authors' hope that these advancements will lay the groundwork for the creation of truly general AI intelligence. The source code for the mentioned projects can be accessed at https://github.com/matt-grefenstienne/GG- Sap/tree/master/2022/02/17. An interactive demonstration showcasing the interpreters' capabilities can be viewed at https://gg-sap.github.io/2022/02/17/. Both the code and the demonstration provide a comprehensive examination of the key difficulties encountered in the project, as well as the technical methods employed and the empirical findings obtained. Ultimately, these advancements are being pursued not for their own sake, but rather as a means of facilitating human understanding through theoretical analysis. It is only when language is treated as a part of a larger philosophical framework, as opposed to a mere collection of data to be analyzed, that true intellectual comprehension can be achieved. For the Electron-Ion Collider's next phase, advancements in silicon technology are being accelerated to meet the collider's complex requirements. 
Precision silicon sensors used in collider experiments must be able to operate in extremely harsh radiation environments. 
To meet the Electron-Ion Collider's stringent low-energy background constraints while being exposed to intense luminosities and radiation levels, researchers are developing advanced silicon technology. 
A cutting-edge silicon sensor prototype, designed for the COMET experiment, is being developed using 3D sensor technology to increase sensitivity. 
This 3D sensor's segmented pillars help in identifying charged particles' creation locations and enhance background suppression capabilities. 
Preliminary testing of this sensor has confirmed its ability to effectively eliminate background noises. 
Future research plans for the sensor are also discussed, which may involve adding active poly Gate technology to enhance the device's performance even further. 
This technology could increase the sensor's sensitivity to very low energy particles, allowing for detection of individual ionization steps. 
Overall, the sensor and technology development is progressing on schedule, and a fully functional system is expected to be implemented by 2022. 
This implementation will play a crucial role in the Electron-Ion Collider's research on the strong nuclear force, delivering critical data on low-energy quantum chromodynamics models. 
Ultimately, the sensor and technology advancements will help the Electron-Ion Collider achieve its goal of achieving precise, quantum-mechanical interpretations of the nuclear's unique properties.

The technique of empirical distribution function estimation for a conditional expectation function has been effective but lacks parametric precision. Nonetheless, using multivariate kernel estimators can achieve asymptotic normality and better results, though it requires specifying greater than minimal variables. In response, this research introduces a hybrid estimator that strikes a balance between simplicity and statistical power, utilizing a degenerate kernel estimator in the unseen variables while employing the empirical distribution function in the seen variables. These gains are demonstrated through convergence rates and asymptotic distributions for key statistics. Furthermore, the methods are substantiated by practical experiments. Interestingly, the findings also illustrate the inadequacies of conventional estimators when dealing with multi-dimensional data. The methodology's applicability in testing hypotheses about the average treatment effect in missing data problems is also explored. Lastly, the methods were implemented using the R programming language, specifically incorporating the crank.nimbl package. Despite its potential drawbacks, the simplicity of these estimators makes them appealing to users. In particular, when dealing with a two-dimensional data set, the proposed estimators were found to be more accurate than conventional methods, while in more complex datasets, the differences became more pronounced. The implementation of these estimators can be seen in the attached code using the R programming language. Specifically, the code uses the crank.nimbl package, recently created by Navarro Strong, which includes functions for estimating conditional expectation functions, among others. The methods' efficacy was assessed through simulation experiments and practical applications, revealing that they often outperformed traditional estimators in various scenarios. Notably, a comparative analysis was conducted between these estimators and those proposed by Polinsky and Walsh, yielding comparable results in some cases and superior performance in others, particularly under more realistic data-generating models. The methods' ability to generalize was also evaluated by generating data from Markov processes, where the sample paths are not only dependent on past values but also possess a stochastic component. In a practical setting, the estimators were applied to analyze the effect of a training program on students' standardized test scores, using data from the Reuber et al study. The findings revealed statistically significant benefits associated with the intervention. We build observers that create a thorough state observation of the SIR model, which is used to simulate the dynamics of infectious disease spread, for both close-to-real and distant observations. This design involves developing an adaptive observer with a nonlinear adaptation component for near-state observation and a linear adaptation component for less accurate initial conditions. Both observer designs successfully produce precise state estimates, achieving a precise error convergence to the equilibrium state within a finite time frame. Numerical simulations demonstrate and validate the effectiveness of these observers in the SIR model for various scenario conditions. Given its generic method approach, this construct can also be applied to other predictive models on population dynamics.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for maintaining knowledge graphs up-to-date with new information. The graph's evolution over time creates temporal edges indicating the arrival of new facts, but automating this process is complicated by the low frequency of these events, leaving human experts overwhelmed. Our proposed solution leverages advancements in language modeling to aid in connection prediction in temporal knowledge graphs, particularly by employing a translated adapter model. This approach consists of two network architectures: a language-model-based adapter, pre-trained on chronological text, and a multi-layer perceptron, to predict new temporal edges and their corresponding attributes. Our adapter model is further refined by fine-tuning it on specific knowledge graphs using a few strategic rationalizations about the graph's structure. Through experiments on diverse datasets, we demonstrate that our method excels at temporal knowledge graph completion, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches. The adaptation of our technique to new graph evaluations shows the potential of pre-trained models in this application. An implementation of the research is available on GitHub. The paper has been successfully peer-reviewed and reviewed at the 2022 Workshop on Text Data Science. Additional details are provided in a supplementary report.

The development of high-power ultrafast lasers depends heavily on Kerr-lens mode-locking, which requires precise electrical current control to establish and maintain a Kerr-lens nonlinear feedback loop. This loop, achieved through a nonlinear optical material's focal length adjustment, enables the generation of ultrafast pulses. This work focuses on the geometric analysis of the electrical current's interaction with the optical cavity in a Kerr-lens mode-locked laser. By describing the electrical current's effect using Green's function and examining multi-beam propagation with nonlinear feedback, researchers have found that mode-locking is heavily influenced by transverse electrical field interactions. As electrical power increases, higher-order frequency modes within the optical cavity become more significant, necessitating a deeper understanding of Kerr-lens mode-locking for the generation of high-power, high-repetition-rate pulse lasers. Applications of optical parametric chiral soliton laser (OPCSL) technology, featuring all-optical mode locking, have also been explored and compared to electrical Kerr-lens mode locking for the development of next-generation pulse lasers. Potential areas of improvement for the electrical current's role in Kerr-lens mode locking are discussed, along with predicted advancements using electrical current control and novel laser designs such as curved and nested cavities. Finally, researchers have identified a promising strategy to achieve even higher pulse energies using scalable OPCSL technology. Despite the achievements of electrical current control, researchers have found that theoretical scaleabilities of both techniques diverge from experimental data, indicating room for innovation in electrical current applications and predictions for the theoretical boundaries of Kerr-lens mode locking. Ultimately, electrical current control offers a versatile tool for the precise manipulation of nonlinear optical interactions and achieves remarkable scaleability in OPCSL technology. However, further research into electrical current effects on the nonlinear optical cavity may yield even more impressive theoretical and practical outcomes. The interaction between electrical current and optical noise within the cavity presents an exciting opportunity for the development of novel OPCS-LASER architectures that could increase the theoretical and practical boundaries of pulse energy and chirp rates, paving the way for an even more impressive scaleable OPCSL technology. As such, electrical current control presents a promising avenue for further innovation in the development of optical lasers. A revolutionary machine learning technique allows models to train on edge devices and learn from shared data without moving it, but a major challenge lies in managing resource limitations on these devices. Traditional methods typically focus on linear regression and don't address the varying computational and power resources found on real-edge devices such as smartphones and GPUs. As a result, they often yield subpar performance and can overuse or underutilize available resources. In this paper, we address these issues by introducing an asynchronous, distributed, and adaptive FL framework called ADIFT, which optimizes nonlinear regression. ADIFT is unique because it allows for concurrent communication and computation, dynamically adjusts learning parameters based on device performance, and utilizes a scalable, clustered communication strategy that reduces latency. ADIFT also incorporates an innovative strategy to detect and adapt to changes in device performance. Extensive testing has shown that ADIFT outperforms existing frameworks, achieving up to a 37% reduction in training time, using standard machine learning datasets and simulated edge device configurations. Our research represents a significant step towards developing a flexible, efficient, and adaptive FL framework that can effectively utilize available resources on real-edge devices. This knowledge can be applied in various contexts to improve the efficiency of non-linear regression models on edge devices and is available under an open-source license. Predicting links in social networks is a vital yet complex task that involves making informed predictions about future social connections.  The challenge lies in capturing the nuanced, context-dependent nature of connection preferences within the network.  Existing frameworks, such as Multiple Poisson Regressions, have treated different nodes' relationship dimensions as separate variables, ignoring the distinct characteristics of individual nodes.  As a result, this approach has suffered from poor predictive performance and inefficient use of available features.  To address these limitations, we introduce SSNE, a novel Embarrassingly Simple Neural Solver for predicting links in networks.  By combining a sophisticated, representation-rich node embedding system with a refined prediction model, SSNE is able to efficiently utilize available features and produce accurate predictions.  In experiments using 14 diverse social networks, SSNE has outperformed existing solutions, such as Multiple Poisson Regressions and Bi-Way Regressions, across multiple performance metrics.  SSNE achieves better predictive accuracy and requires lower computational overhead than existing solutions, such as Bi-Way Regressions, while also efficiently using available features.  SSNE is a suitable solution for predicting links in social networks.  The code for SSNE is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/PangJiao/SSNE. We develop a generalized model to address the issue of recovering nonuniform sparse signals, and our proposed method, NuSPAN, utilizes a Proximal Mean Network to achieve this task. By integrating a learned proximal operator into a traditional Mean Estimation model, NuSPAN is shown to be capable of accurately recovering both uniform and nonuniform sparse signals. Furthermore, NuSPAN is engineered to enhance the learning of its proximal operator, making it a more efficient and effective method. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NuSPAN through its application in seismic reflectivity recovery, where it is compared to traditional sparse seismic inversion techniques. Our experimental results reveal that NuSPAN is able to strike a balance between sparsity and energy fidelity, and its use of a learned proximal operator allows for seamless adaptation to varying signal characteristics. We also investigate the computational efficiency of NuSPAN, finding that its proximity loss enhances training speed, and its application in seismic reflection data results in seismic depth imaging models that are both sparse and visually appealing. Moreover, NuSPAN's ability to handle nonuniform signals enables the accurate reconstruction of intricate subsurface structures, thereby enhancing the accuracy of seismic inversion. We anticipate that the design of NuSPAN can inspire the development of additional sparsity-encouraging network architectures for diverse machine learning applications. The proposed model involves a sequence-to-set predictor, evaluated on Italian historical documents, and demonstrates high reliability, specifically achieving an 87% probability of including the correct tag, as well as a mean absolute error of 1.64. Additionally, the probability distribution of the top two tags includes the correct tag in around 94% of the cases. Furthermore, the proposed approach exhibits robust performance even in the presence of noisy labels, and it is versatile, allowing it to be used in other historical document annotation tasks beyond part-of-speech tagging. Urban planning expectations frequently arise from diverse sources like focus group discussions, social media, and public comments, which expectators express in various formats. Managing these numerous, often conflicting, expectations poses a significant challenge for city officials, primarily due to the difficulty in understanding what citizens truly expect after analyzing their verbal statements and feedback forms. To streamline this process, we developed an automated Expectation Management Assistant that formalizes and prioritizes city dwellers' diverse expectations. To address the initial phase, we constructed an NLP-based system to convert expectations into a structured specification in a city planning context. Our approach involves generating expectations in a certain format, identifying expected outcomes, and translating these into a usable format for city officials. We evaluated our assistant through a simulation test on a dataset comprising over 2000 expectations extracted from Reddit discussions about NYC. Our evaluation demonstrated that a significant majority (85%) of expectations could be expressed in a standardized, formal manner, with around 8 out of 10 being complete and comprehensible specifications. Our study highlights the potential of using automated tools to convert city planning expectations into a usable and manageable format for city officials. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/mitkovitz/SmartExpectation. Our work was supported by the Smart Cities research group at the NYU Tandon School of Engineering. Future work should focus on the second phase of expectation management - resource allocation - where we plan to develop a system that enables city officials to select the most important expectations and assign resources accordingly. Additionally, future research should aim to further develop our NLP model to handle more city-specific expectations. What's more, integrating our Expectation assistant into a full-fledged urban planning information system infrastructure is another crucial step in the expectation management process. Our work is part of a broader effort to develop urban infrastructure as a service platform. Our expectation management tool can be a key module within this platform, where city officials can upload and manage expectations that have been converted into a standardized format. Our goal is to work closely with city officials to further develop this tool and make it a part of a comprehensive city data management system. To achieve this, we are exploring the feasibility of deploying our Expectation assistant on a cloud-based infrastructure (e.g. OpenShift) to enable the deployment of city-specific instances for local governments to use. Our future research will entail collaborating with city officials to incorporate our Expectation assistant into the UBI platform (a national infrastructure for urban planning) as a prototype demo. In the vast library of human DNA, analyzing sequences to identify patterns or relationships proves challenging due to its massive size and diversity, despite advances in sequencing technology. A crucial research area is developing methods for automatically representing similar DNA sequences with similar concepts. To accomplish this, unsupervised learning of sequence representations from large genomic databases is a promising strategy. By applying an unsupervised learning method to a large dataset of sequences, similar sequences can be represented closely together in a new space, while dissimilar sequences are repelled from each other, allowing for automated discovery of underlying relationships. However, due to the natural variability in DNA sequences, a challenging gradient descent-based approach is difficult to find. To overcome this, sequence representations can be generated initially and then compared with a corresponding binary code using a noisy autosencoder, where the noise-introduced codes are close to each other in the new space. We propose an improved variant of this approach, referred to as Genomic Binary Autosencoder (GBA), combining a greedy method for selecting key features with an efficient noisy autosencoder for recognizing similar sequences. By testing our proposed method on three distinct datasets, our results show that GBA is effective in identifying concepts within genomic sequences. Furthermore, a comparison with existing methods highlights that GBA produces sequences with fewer variations while identifying longer patterns. Importantly, the sequences generated by our method are interpretable and can be visualized to better understand the relationships between similar sequences. Finally, our research demonstrates that by applying our method to various genomic sequences, the resulting representations are highly diverse and reflect different biological processes such as operon regulation in bacteria. These results suggest the potential of using unsupervised learning of sequence representations to identify underlying relationships within genomic data. Moreover, our method provides a significant framework for analyzing genomic sequences, similar to how word embeddings provide insights into language semantics. Ultimately, our sequence representations can be exploited to enhance our understanding of fundamental bacterial processes, such as operon regulation, protein translation, and DNA replication. Conservation laws under certain conditions can be disrupted by small conserved quantities. A new approach has been developed for addressing these discrepancies in a wide range of equations applicable to solid mechanics, electromagnetism, and fluid dynamics. The developed technique is particularly innovative as it allocates unique physical attributes to additional variables not present in the original conservation laws. For confirming its applicability in fluid dynamics, a new framework has been introduced for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. A subsequent dual mapping has been implemented for perturbing and then recovering the conservation laws, which in turn enabled deriving explicit formulas for stabilizers and a unique Lyapunov function for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. Similar techniques have been employed in recent studies on electromagnetism and solid mechanics to derive Lyapunov functions for the corresponding equations. A related technological framework, known as Conservative Modification Framework (CMF), has been developed for automated generation of stabilizer and Lyapunov functions in scenarios involving conservation law perturbations. CMF has been successfully demonstrated with multiple case studies in fields such as fluid dynamics, electromagnetism, and solid mechanics. A major goal of this method is to provide rigorous mathematical proofs for a broad range of dynamic models, which in turn may lead to potential applications in various fields. A demonstration is provided on how the technique can be effectively applied to extract Lyapunov function candidates using entropy as an underlying principle. A related project, known as Conservative Modification Repository (CMR), has been developed for storing and sharing mathematical models with broken conservation laws, accompanied by suggestions for their repair. Recent advancements in ML have led to a surge in research interest, with the goal of identifying, categorizing, and predicting numeric and non-numeric variables based on numerous real-world applications. In this research, several supervised and unsupervised ML algorithms were applied to the Numerical dataset to achieve classification. The findings demonstrate that supervised ML algorithms performed better on the given dataset, producing accurate results. Meanwhile, the feasibility of pruning ML algorithms was explored, focusing on the feature selection method (FS). Comparing the results of 30 features and 13 ML algorithms, the analysis identified the most relevant features contributing to accuracy. Interestingly, the analysis showed that both relevant and irrelevant features impact accuracy, albeit in different contexts. Ultimately, the research recommendations for the selected ML algorithm with high accuracy are presented. As such, this study aims to contribute to the ML classification field by assessing algorithms' performance and analyzing feature importance on the Numa dataset.

To minimize the risk of COVID-19 transmission, accurate and efficient diagnosis is critical, particularly for patients with suspected symptoms. Computed Tomography (CT) scans can help identify the virus by highlighting infections in the lungs. Scanning at higher resolutions yields more detailed images but increases radiation exposure, refinement typically requiring the processing of larger image sets. This study aims to optimize the detection of COVID-19 in low-dose computed tomography using a time-distributed capsule network architecture. The approach involves splitting image processing and classification into separate two-stage processes, allowing for deeper networks and increased capacity for feature extraction. This enhanced capsule network architecture achieves detection competency with lower radiation doses and reduced scanning times, thus enhancing the probability of accurate diagnoses while minimizing the risks associated with prolonged scanning. Experimental outcomes indicate that our method outperforms existing techniques in terms of area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and accuracy (ACC) on the Emory Semantics CV19 challenge dataset. Furthermore, other critical metrics including loss, AUC at 95% confidence, AUC, precision, recall, and F1-score were also found to improve as a result of this implementation. This algorithm has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/jeedahassan/TCNN. The study's results and analysis are compiled in a submitted paper to the Emory Semantics CV19 challenge. The challenge's leaderboard currently reports the following key metrics: AUC: 0.9721, precision: 0.9706, recall: 0.9701, F1-score: 0.9701, ACC: 0.9701. The study's results and analysis are compiled in a submitted paper to Medical Image Analysis. Key considerations for space utilization include: 
- Addressing potential deployment difficulties for large spacecraft in LEO, such as those necessary for solar power stations or giant radio telescopes. 
- Identifying feasible deployment methods and strategies for satellites and other space objects. 
- Exploring the feasibility of using smaller spacecraft or "fleyby" structures that could be used as temporary or permanent platforms in LEO, such as those for solar power stations or radio telescopes, as an alternative to full-sized spacecraft.

This research study focuses on the space exploration aspect, given its potential to expand humanity's presence in the solar system and mitigate planetary risks.

- To achieve a high level of temporary platform space utilization when launching multiple small spacecraft instead of one large one, we must prioritize the weight distribution of these spacecraft. 
- Using multiple small spacecraft with variable masses may provide the best outcome, as this configuration allows for greater maneuverability.

Mesh creation for finite element methods is an essential process that is typically generated using a refinement process from a initial coarse mesh. This paper presents a novel method to build high-order meshes directly from CAD models, bypassing the need for an initial coarse mesh. The proposed approach utilizes linear optimization with whole number variables to create refined meshes with various orders of refinement, including both standard and irregular quadrilateral meshes. By leveraging the capabilities of modern mesh optimization tools, the resulting meshes are highly optimized, featuring elements with optimal characteristics that are well-suited for numerical computations. The presented method demonstrates the creation of high-order meshes, including up to C1 continuous meshes with 2000-3000 elements, that are generated in under an hour and demonstrate superior numerical performance compared to lower-order meshes. The created meshes are further utilized in a benchmark test to illustrate the method's ability to produce highly-optimized quadrilateral meshes. The implementation of this method is provided on the GitHub platform under the repository https://github.com/autonomousmeshcreation/Linear_Optimization_Fine_Meshing. The mesh creation process is demonstrated in the video available at https://youtu.be/4QrYsF_9Guc. The created meshes are visualized through the video available at https://youtu.be/6Mm314R0A8E. The method's potential applications and future work are also discussed, including the current limitations of the method such as its incompatibility with complex quadrilateral meshes and its current inability to handle meshes with hanging nodes without significant increase in computational cost and complexity. The presented research provides the foundation for further investigations into generation of high-order meshes from CAD models and expands the scope of mesh creation methods, particularly the generation of high-order coarse quadrilateral meshes in both FEM and FWEC contexts. The research also promotes the development of more efficient and practical methods for creating high-order meshes from direct from CAD models. The presented method's current drawbacks in performance and flexibility are acknowledged, and the creation of more robust and efficient methods is proposed as future work, with the goal of reducing the computational cost and increasing the geometric flexibility of the method. To address this, we've developed the LitMind Lexicon, a comprehensive, publicly-accessible dictionary that incorporates context-driven examples to enhance word comprehension. By incorporating 2.7 billion examples and utilizing our proprietary context separation technique to avoid overfitting, the Lexicon has achieved superior performance in benchmark tests. Furthermore, the LitMind Lexicon serves as a meaningful example of how language instruction can benefit from an advanced, data-driven approach. We'll detail the process behind our dictionary's creation, as well as demonstrate its potential for real-world applications in automated writing, customized education content, and advanced research tools. Given the restrictions of traditional publishing formats, we've created the LitMind Lexicon as a digital resource, available at www.litmindlex.com, and accompanied it with an open-source coding foundation at www.github.com/LitMindLEx. To ensure seamless browsing, the Lexicon's digital interface adapts to user queries, employing strategies like automatic word suggestions, dynamic query logging, and intuitive query expansion to strike a balance between comprehensive results and clutter-free presentation. An exemplar is the word 'domino effect', for which users can access multiple example sentences, word definitions, associated imagery, geotagged locations, and audio recordings. To facilitate global understanding, the Lexicon's query interface translates the user's natural language into a standard, universal code (URC), enabling words to be recognized regardless of linguistic variations. In this paper, we'll illustrate the underlying logic of our dictionary's response to two real-world queries submitted via the website. As a result, the Lexicon has completed over 100 million inquiries from roughly 190 countries and territories since its public release in 2018. Recent research introduced LIME-RS, a region-based algorithm that uses sampling to improve the computational efficiency of LIME, making it suitable for applications with high dimensionality and complex data. However, the LIME-RS model's local interpretations of recommendation data raised concerns about its effectiveness. This study assesses the LIME-RS model's validity for such complex data and explores ways to enhance its consistency. Building on the idea that human-generated metadata can improve the perturbation method's accuracy, particularly for time-based data, the authors conducted experiments using various parameters on LIME-RS models applied to two recommendation datasets. They discovered that incorporating domain knowledge significantly increases the model's consistency. This finding underscores the necessity of developing methods that combine optimization techniques with domain-aware perturbation methods to reinforce the LIME-RS model's reliability. Moreover, the authors implemented a new time-related perturbation method that preserves temporal constraints, resulting in a more accurate and consistent model. This novel approach was evaluated using time-based features in the Avito Moscow KPIs dataset. In contrast to the baseline models, the time-based LIME-RS model produced more accurate and consistent interpretations at a significantly lower computational cost. Following extensive user testing, the authors determined that an accurate LIME-RS model with consistent interpretations is typically characterized by small feature importance values, with users preferring such models. Additionally, the authors identified a potential "informational ceiling" where further model refinement may not lead to more accurate and consistent interpretations. This occurrence could be attributed to several factors, such as overfitting or an inefficient perturbation method. We present LIME-RS Consistency, a framework for evaluating the consistency of the LIME-RS model, along with two techniques for enhancing consistency, which were demonstrated on Avito datasets. The authors also showcased the applicability of these methods to a diverse range of neural networks by achieving a 100% consistent model for the CoFiNet dataset. The authors conducted experiments across multiple datasets, achieving a 100% consistent model for the CoFiNet dataset. The surface electronic properties of materials have significant implications for the functionality of quantum wells and nanostructures. InSb and InAs quantum wells are prominent examples of narrow bandgap materials with unique surface electronic properties, but the interplay between these surfaces and their bulk properties is complex. By integrating GaSb substrates with a layer structure that includes an InAs epilayer, researchers can observe the emergence of a well-defined InAs quantum well at the surface while minimizing the contribution from the GaSb substrate. Using XPS scanning and spectroscopy, researchers can precisely pinpoint the well's position. Notably, a crucial step in these measurements, the surface preparation process, can unexpectedly push the InAs quantum well deeper into the epilayer due to macroscopic surface roughness. To mitigate this issue, researchers can employ an ultra-vacuum annealing process that resurfaces the sample and enables accurate positioning of the InAs quantum well at the interface using a precise depth profiling technique, combined with the analysis of a distinctive substrate peak. Furthermore, this technique allows for the identification of a quantum well's polarization orientation based on the presence of a distinct As peak. To advance quantum information processing, sophisticated single-chip devices are being developed that combine different quantum systems, such as semiconductor single electrons, superconducting circuits, and spin systems, operating at distinct temperature and energy ranges. A key aim is to integrate these various quantum components on a single chip, particularly when interacting locally. However, the intricate interference between different quantum states complicates the understanding of their individual behaviors. By analyzing these interactions, it's feasible to distinguish between distinct quantum coupling mechanisms. A method to distinguish between different types of interactions between a quantum point contact and a superconducting region in a triple gate structure is presented. Utilizing real-time tracking of the quantum point, this approach differentiates between multiple potential mechanisms for charge tunneling. Notably, it's been found that the presence of a localized spin in the tunneling region doesn't provide sufficient evidence to distinguish between these various scenarios. Consequently, this technique can be applied broadly to other hybrid quantum systems, such as spin-superconducting, and double quantum point contacts coupled to multiple magnetic regions. Furthermore, this methodology could potentially identify the presence of a dark mode in a system interacting with multiple qubits. A related issue is also explored, such as calculating the influence of a superconducting island coupled to multiple triangular quantum points on the real-time tracking of charge in the bulk. This research lays the groundwork for identifying the quantum correlation between distinct systems, such as a superconducting region and a quantum point contact, and could be applied to other hybrid quantum systems. It's also demonstrated that the proposed technique to distinguish between various types of interactions in a particular configuration isn't affected by its extension to a larger network of quantum components. However, the interaction between different quantum systems and their real-time tracking poses technical difficulties, such as potential thermal fluctuations and noise influencing detector precision. Ultimately, the experimental implementation of the method depends on overcoming these challenges. A related concern, such as calculating the impact of a quantum point contact on real-time charge monitoring in a superconducting triode, is also examined. This research opens the door for further investigation into the integration of multiple quantum systems on a single chip and the exploration of their combined behavior. It's also notable that the interaction between these various quantum components can be interpreted as a collective behavior of their individual constituents. Deep learning-based frameworks, particularly Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO), have become the go-to choice for addressing complex audio retrieval challenges. However, the need for MIMO architectures, which require parallel processing of multiple inputs, is still unclear. This question arises not only for audio retrieval but also for general deep learning practices, so we seek to answer it by studying the effectiveness of MIMO architectures. Our answer lies in a in-depth analysis of MIMO networks, where we demonstrate the merit of MIMO architectures by showing the benefit of feature sharing and exchange among networks, either through direct sharing or by aggregating features and swapping them among networks. This shared knowledge, we found, enhances model performance by allowing incorporation of global information into individual networks. Our analysis, which uses convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and MIMO versions of CNNs (MIMONet) on the VGG Sound dataset, reveals the significance of feature exchange in MIMONet performance. Moreover, by introducing a global information enhancement layer in MIMONet, we can determine the optimal ratio of shared features and contribute the framework, known as Multi-Input Multi-Output Net (MIMONet), which can aid in a deeper comprehension of MIMO architectures and improve MIMONet performance. We introduce a new axiom system, called timed definitions, within the HOL theorem prover, which combines recursion and imperative-style state-based programming. This approach extends HOL's recursive function domain typing to accommodate state parameters, effectively viewed as additional recursive arguments. Our tailored axiom system ensures soundness with respect to HOL, confirming that timed definitions correspond to traditional recursive functions. Moreover, we develop a proof translation mechanism, allowing for the transformation of a timed definition into an equivalent recursive function within HOL. This contributes to the feasibility of proving timed definitions within HOL, providing a framework for verifying critical timing-related software components. Additionally, we provide evidence of the effectiveness of our approach through the formal verification of a state-based implementation of the classic Misra algorithm for generating invariants in while-programs, which had previously presented challenges to formal proof due to its explicit state management and recursive structure. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of representing timed concepts within HOL, bridging the gap between theoretical and implementational proofs. Furthermore, we examine the applicability of our approach to other marked theorem provers, specifically Isabelle and Coq, which offer more advanced automation features but pose difficulties due to their lack of built-in state management. Although the use of timed definitions within these provenance-based frameworks presents new axiomatization challenges, our previous work on HOL provides a potential solution. Ultimately, our investigation contributes to the exploration of integrated imperative and functional programming within theoretical proof assistants, potentially extending to other formal verification tools. This research originates from a thorough evaluation of Isabelle's state-based programming techniques as part of a formal proof of the fundamental theorem in Polya's theory of inductive recursion, which necessitated the incorporation of imperative reasoning to manage the recursion structure, which could potentially be replaced with a purely functional solution, sparking a investigation into the interplay between imperative and functional programming within theoretical proof assistants. The HOL implementation presented in this work is based on a previous state-of-the-art implementation by the author in Isabelle. The HOL implementation represents a novel application of our earlier axiom system to a marked theorem prover, which provides further insights into the feasibility of combined imperative and functional programming across these platforms. This could potentially extend to other formal verification tools, should they permit such combinations. A pre-recorded video of this work is available at https://youtu.be/ggF2t1dii5Y.

Results from both numerical and experimental approaches demonstrate that shielding is prominently exhibited at resonance frequencies that align with the electronic transitions within the granular substrate. Moreover, simulations reveal that this shielding phenomenon can be attributed to the synchronized oscillations between magnetic dipoles and electric dipoles present in the substrate. These findings not only provide an understanding of the anomalous shielding effect but also offer a case study on the application of electromagnetic induction in granular substances. Ultimately, this presents an opportunity to explore novel applications based on this effect, specifically in the realm of nanotechnology and ultra-low frequency electromagnetic biology, while also contributing to the understanding of electromagnetic interactions within complex media. This model reveals that Sgr A East resulted from a $30\pm 10$ M$_\odot$ supernova caused by a binary collision resulting from a binary system that was once an O star and a black hole. The extensive masses observed for the B-field star population in the Sgr A* vicinity, ranging from approximately 3 to 20 M$_\odot$, strongly suggest the existence of an additional, yet undiscovered population of stars near Sgr A*. Incorporating the newly found star counts, our model indicates that the Sgr A East explosion occurred about 3.8 kiloparsecs from Sgr A*. This location closely matches the center of the Sgr A East nebula, further supporting our findings. The vast difference in mass between the Sgr A East supernova and those found at the edges of the nebula further reinforces our model that the Sgr A East explosion was the result of a stellar collision, rather than a single star supernova. Lastly, our model highlights a critical requirement: the previously undiscovered stars near Sgr A* must be observed at a very early stage in their development. Future VLT/PDLF observations should be able to verify these newly discovered B-field stars and confirm our initial hypothesis. If confirmed, our model would imply that the Sgr A East supernova occurred about 80 years prior to the current observation, providing clear evidence that the Sgr A* vicinity has not yet experienced any star formation. Additionally, our model would suggest that the Sgr A* mass accumulation began around the 1940s and would require the Sgr A* black hole to have been emitting tens of thousands of radio signals throughout the past century, many of which went undetected. Ultimately, these findings would imply that the Sgr A* vicinity remains in a state of complete star silence. Imbalanced data distribution frequently occurs in real-world applications and can lead to biased outcomes when left untreated. The field of text classification is particularly vulnerable to class imbalance, which can result from the rarity of certain keywords in some categories, making the learning process challenging. One strategy to improve model performance on unbalanced data involves oversampling majority classes, but a proposed method seeks to optimize oversampling by integrating word frequencies. By generating more diverse instances and reducing dependence on rare words, this approach aims to enhance the overall performance of text classification models. Following this, a BERT-based method is introduced to compare the effectiveness of the presented method and two popular artificial oversampling techniques for multi-category text classification tasks. The experiments indicate that the proposed method outperforms the other two techniques, showcasing its feasibility and efficacy in improving text classification models. The results also show that incorporating domain knowledge into the training process of text classification models through the use of ontology can lead to improved accuracy and a higher f1 score, particularly for the third category in this study. However, using ontology alone did not solve the classification problem, but when combined with the proposed artificial oversampling technique for unbalanced data, it achieved the highest overall f1 score among all the methods tested. The research highlights that simply incorporating domain knowledge does not address the challenge of unbalanced data without the need for additional preprocessing. Moreover, artificial oversampling proved to be an effective method to balance data distribution in this case, enabling the learning of domain knowledge through the presentation of more diverse data to the model. Ultimately, domain knowledge plays a crucial role in determining model performance in this context, leading to potentially improved outcomes with the integration of oversampling. The presented findings suggest that domain knowledge and oversampling can be synergistic, leading to improved model performance. The code for the research has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/76855 bert-text-classification. The primary dataset utilized in the study, consisting of product comments from an online retail company, was provided by the dataset owner for experimental purposes. The research demonstrates that artificial oversampling can effectively address the challenge of unbalanced data distribution in text classification tasks. The method integrates word frequencies to optimize oversampling and increase the diversity of generated instances. By presenting these insights, the research contributes to the advancement of classification systems by addressing data imbalance through a novel oversampling technique that enhances the overall performance of text classification models. The research further demonstrates that domain knowledge can lead to improved model performance in text classification tasks, especially when combined with artificial oversampling. primarily attributed to the newly discovered Omicron variant.  The rapid spread of coronavirus
in the U.S. is partly fueled by inadequate public understanding and adherence to safety protocols.
The role of regional media outlets is pivotal in disseminating vital information about COVID-19
to their audiences, employing novel digital technologies like augmented reality (AR) to enhance
informative content.  This study leverages a web scraper to collect data from 138 regional news
websites spanning 23 states, examining the relationship between COVID-19-related content, digital
platforms, and infections across the U.S. and individual states, including the impact of AR-enabled
content on case rates and fatalities.  The proposed framework will enable research into the interplay
between COVID-19, digital technology, and local news sources, opening doors for potential interventions
aimed at mitigating the coronavirus's further spread through augmented reality-enabled communication. 
The research demonstrates that data-driven approaches can generate new research questions, offering a
pathway for future studies on information technology and medical epidemics.  The research data and code
are available on GitHub at https://github.com/gtiffel/Regional-COVID-News. 
By analyzing 23,831 articles and 3,53,851 reader comments from 138 regional news sites over a
three-week period starting in mid-February, the research discovered a positive correlation between
COVID-related content and Omicron cases across the U.S, but no correlation was discovered between
regional news and cases or fatalities in individual states.  It was also found that polarized discussion
was more prevalent in states with higher COVID-related content.  The study further demonstrated that
states with greater use of augmented reality-enabled tools experienced lower case rates but no correlation
was discovered between AR-enabled content and fatalities.  The research shows that augmented reality
has the potential to be a positive force in raising public awareness about COVID-19. 
Ultimately, the research highlights the need for increased awareness and adherence to safety protocols
to contain the coronavirus's further spread. 
It was also discovered that digital platforms play a vital role in disseminating information about COVID-19 to their audiences. 
The study concluded that the rapid spread of the virus could be halted if regional news outlets effectively communicated crucial information about COVID-19 to their audiences using innovative digital technologies like augmented reality (AR).

To better understand complex systems influenced by random factors, researchers are utilizing stochastic versions of existing Hamiltonian systems to describe their dynamics. Although the stochastic process generated is often Gaussian and continuous in space, its short-term trajectory is inherently discrete and unpredictable, displaying characteristics of statistical indeterminacy. A recent development involves applying the geometric Hamiltonian stochastic process framework, proposed by Keller and Ottobre (2010), to analyze systems like the 1D and 3D isotropic Gaussian processes, as well as the 1D harmonic oscillator. Building upon this foundation, this study explores Gaussian stochastic process manifolds in one and three dimensions, detailing their differential structure and providing short-term velocity estimates, ultimately leading to a computational strategy for obtaining geodesic approximations. A non-parametric approach based on Fourier series is employed to demonstrate the feasibility of calculating geodesics even with limited data, as demonstrated through a 1D analysis of the harmonic oscillator and Lorenz system. Moreover, a 3D evaluation of the Lorenz equations reveals the potential for significant improvements in geodesic approximations when data is augmented. As the accuracy of these geodesic estimates depends on the residual random noise, this study ultimately delves into the inherent duality between stochastic process manifolds and their geometric counterparts, proposing a systematic framework for recovering the underlying analytic geodesic curves of a Gaussian stochastic process. A compactness criterion based on Fourier series is established to achieve this goal, as well as explore the theoretical and practical implications of this method in relation to the limit cycle behavior of the Lorenz system. Future research is anticipated to involve the development of more accurate methods for recovering geodesic curves, particularly in systems where high precision is essential, potentially requiring the integration of machine learning methods. A demonstration of this approach's potential is provided through an application of the Fourier method to the recovery of geodesic curves in a 1D analysis of the Lorenz system. A thorough examination of remaining challenges and open questions in this field allows for the identification of promising avenues for future investigation. These include the feasibility of applying geometric stochastic process frameworks to markovian Markov processes, as well as the potential for uncovering desirable properties in systems designed to be Hamiltonian. This research outlines a field-split nonlinear preconditioner designed to expedite Navier-Stokes solutions during two-phase flow simulations through porous media, adhering to conservation of mass and momentum. In contrast to conventional Newton-type methods, this approach linearizes the residual with respect to pressures and velocities, resulting in separate preconditioners. When implemented in conjunction with an iterative solver for pressure and a direct solver for velocity, computational efficiency is significantly improved. To illustrate the efficacy of this preconditioner, we examined and compared it with a Newton-based approach using extensive 2D and 3D simulations of single-phase flow and two-phase flow via primary-degree finite elements. Notably, we discovered that when achieving a comparable level of precision, the nonlinear preconditioner requires substantially more time at each iteration than a Newton-based method, mainly due to the need for multiple linear system solves. Nonetheless, since Newton-based methods generally require more iterations to achieve the same level of precision, the nonlinear preconditioner has the potential to yield substantial overall performance improvements. Specifically, in a 200x200 mesh 2D case, we observed that the nonlinear preconditioner requires 2-3 times the computational resources of a Newton-based method while offering the advantage of guaranteed convergence and reduced memory usage. Similarly, in a 50x50 3D case, the nonlinear preconditioner required 4-6 times the computational resources of a Newton-based method, although it was better suited to parallel processing due to its increased memory demands. In terms of code efficiency, the direct solver used for the preconditioner turned out to be the rate-limiting factor, accounting for more than 90% of the computational resources, despite further optimization potential. Subsequent testing of the algorithms on a Quaternary processor revealed that using fine-mesh models would lead to a significant slowdown, emphasizing the need for sparse-matrix solvers that can handle the more efficient compression and parallelization. We verify this connection through the integration of a modified Liouville stress tensor over a specific tetrahedron and, as an alternative validation, demonstrate that the main proposal and this relation can also be derived from a matrix framework based on the light-cone world-sheet action of a Polyakov path integral. Our work provides additional evidence for the connection between certain Liouville CFT and JT gravity theories. It ultimately enables the formulation of new relationships involving the correlation functions of Liouville CFT's non-linear sigma model and the action of JT gravity, thereby offering insights into the behavior of quantum gravity. We perform numerical computations to verify that the power series expansion of the gravity action converges within a specified radius of convergence, which corresponds to a well-known restriction on the validity of the Neumann-Neumann gauge in Liouville CFT. We further observe that this expression has an alternative representation as a weighted sum over the discrete set of integers. We ultimately argue that this finding points to the existence of a Neumann-Dirichlet gauge for Liouville CFT, which might have implications for understanding the behavior of the gravity action at late times within the jordanian tetrahedron framework. Our research finds that relying solely on binary classification of contextual validity is insufficient for full recovery and proposes an enhanced approach that provides more comprehensive feedback to the model. By generating a custom score for each term's relevance, our framework enables the model to learn more precise relationships between words and entities. Additionally, our work highlights the significance of terms that support identified entities in creating coherent context, a phenomenon that requires further exploration. The main contributions of our study are the adoption of a more informative feedback mechanism, the separation of binary and full recovery tasks, and the emergence of contextual NER as a promising foundation for future research. In medical settings, clinicians often face challenges when processing the large volumes of information available to each patient. This consideration of multiple factors is crucial in identifying comorbidities and providing comprehensive, data-driven suggestions. However, the complexity of medical data and the need for diverse comparisons can make it difficult to identify similar patients. One potential solution is to utilize graph neural networks, which can model relationships within individual patients. However, the current state of the art typically assumes that graph edges are already expert-defined, which is not the case in medical settings. As a result, we propose GS-GNN, a novel graph similar network that leverages diverse similarity graph edges trained end-to-end. This approach utilizes a variant of Maximal Margin Discrete Integration to ensure patient similarity is estimated from multiple perspectives. An empirical evaluation of GS-GNN was conducted using a commercial health insurance company's data, demonstrating its ability to accurately predict patient similarities and apply its results to predictive health modeling. The proposed method was shown to outperform traditional graph neural networks that rely on pre-defined edges, as well as other comparative approaches. Additionally, we have made our code available on GitHub. With the continued growth of digital medical records, graph similarity models such as GS-GNN have the potential to maximize the benefits of predictive medical modeling. A parallel processing approach is first used to identify possible transmission paths from non-failed nodes to the destination, with a scheduling algorithm then selecting the most efficient path to maintain signal quality and overall network performance. Unlike other scheduling methods, our solution requires minimal global information, with an efficient encoding scheme then compressing transmission data to minimize energy consumption, thereby increasing battery life for improved overall network efficiency. Numerical results confirm our approach outperforms existing solutions, with our encoding scheme in particular delivering precise energy savings by reducing transmission load. A technique for identifying edges in satellite images is proposed without relying on deep networks. This method employs a combination of two components: A filter with optimal characteristics is applied to extract local maxima along edge fronts, and then either thresholding or backprojection is used to create a binary map. Subsequent processing involves combining information from neighboring pixels to smooth the binary map, and finally, connectivity analysis is used to determine the locations of geometric features in the original image. An algorithm based on this method is presented and demonstrated through its application to a range of satellite images, showcasing its effectiveness. Notably, this technique requires minimal computational resources and can function effectively at any scale, making it highly suitable for real-time applications. Furthermore, the reliance on simple mathematical functions allows for the easy modification of the algorithm's parameters, enabling the targeted identification of specific geometric features. An comparison with a deep network-based method is also conducted to illustrate its advantages. The technique's simplicity and efficiency make it a viable solution for the rapid identification of geometric features in satellite images. Moreover, the flexibility of the algorithm allows for the adaptation of the processing parameters for the optimal detection of specific features in a range of imaging situations. An example of an application of the technique is the automatic detection of road boundaries in high-resolution images of cities. Experimental results illustrate the technique's ability to outperform state-of-the-art methods, including the widely used VGG16 deep network. Notably, the technique's processing time is significantly lower, ranging from 0.8 to 1.3 ms, which is at least 3 to over 200 times faster, respectively. An additional advantage of the technique is its robustness to changes in imaging conditions and feature distributions, making it well-suited for the detection of roads in a variety of urban environments. Overall, the proposed method's simplicity, flexibility, and performance advantages make it a versatile and efficient solution for the identification of geometric features in satellite images. An example of an application of the technique is the automatic extraction of quantitative indices of city spatial organization as demonstrated in the associated video. The average processing time is approximately 1 ms, which enables real-time feedback and subsequent analysis of the binary map's properties. Notably, the technique's compact size and rapid processing time make it well-suited for embedded systems, allowing for the rapid extraction of geometric data and computational models.
