In advanced radiation sensors, malfunction can be triggered by the intense radiation encountered, which may be intended or unintentionally present, increasing the difficulty in achieving reliable machine learning performance. To address this issue, our approach utilizes a combination of generative adversarial networks and conditional GANs in conjunction with ensemble learning. Specifically, this hybrid method comprises a generative adversarial network, a hybrid GAN, and pairwise GANs, all trained to predict radiation modulation classification. When subjected to radiation intensity, this hybrid model exhibits significantly improved stability and accuracy compared to the baseline convolutional neural network, achieving a high classification rate of 0.93, and its runtime is comparable to a convolutional neural network. Enabling the model to function reliably in environments with varying radiation levels is the primary benefit of this approach. Furthermore, our framework is adaptable to various architectures of generative adversarial networks, making it suitable for a wide range of applications. To validate our method, classification results are presented for three distinct radiation modulation types: AM, FM, and PM, as well as a mixed signal containing multiple types of modulation, and these results demonstrate the model's ability to identify multiple types of modulation while withstanding intense radiation interference. Ultimately, our approach of combining generative adversarial networks to predict radiation modulation classification offers a promising solution to machine learning performance resilience against hostile radiation conditions. Moreover, our hybrid framework's accuracy shows minimal decline in its classification performance even when subjected to radiation intensity that is 100 times that of the norm, which is a level of radiation intensity characteristic of commercial space environments. To take this work one step further, our ensemble model is applied to the detection of solar radiation, achieving high accuracy and specificity, which could potentially contribute to a pressing technological gap of deep space solar detection. The major technological limitation of deep space solar detection of late has been the inability to effectively utilize machine learning for high-accuracy solar detection, which our work addresses by achieving high-accuracy solar detection using radiation intensity that is an essential component of this field. Although there is no universally accepted definition of model error in dynamics, the literature indicates it can take on various forms such as model mismatch, approximations in parameter identification processes, random fluctuations in data, and errors arising from computation and measurement limitations. This study proposes a comprehensive framework for conceptualizing model error as a nonlinear dynamic process, thus facilitating the development of innovative methods for adaptive filtering, parameter estimation, and system control design. This work seeks to provide a foundational structure for both theoretical frameworks and practical applications. This research is particularly timely due to the expanding role of AI in generating models, which inevitably incur some error. However, conventional model-based control designs, which rely on error-invariant statistical principles, risk becoming increasingly ineffective in AI-driven models with their increasing Model Error Rate. This trend highlights the need for a paradigmatic shift in control design that accounts for non-stationary model error dynamics, which this research seeks to address by developing dynamic models, estimation techniques, and control designs for varying model error patterns. The frameworks suggested in this research can enhance our understanding of model error as a dynamic process and provide a potential solution to the ongoing debate over the appropriate statistical distribution for learning models. This study provides novel perspectives on model error characterization, its dynamic evolution, distribution fitting, and adaptive learning. The corresponding mathematical theories and engineering designs developed in this research are highly versatile, applicable to various settings, and can also be extended to address additional, intricate topics such as temporal and spatial modeling, and the integration of model error into system models for both theoretical and practical purposes. A particular type of molecular cloud known as Infrared Dark Clouds (IRDCs) is assumed to be the progenitor of Massive Star Forming Clouds (MSFCs), yet the transformation of an IRDC into a MSFC is not fully understood. The study presented here focuses on one of the largest and most massive clouds observed so far - a 1 degree wide dark feature called the Dragon - to explore the evolution of cloud cores within it. This investigation employed the 12 mm continuum observations of the cloud, along with the capability to map the entropy of the dust in these cores. The analysis revealed at least 17 cores within the cloud, with eight of them being more evolved than others due to increased temperatures. One of these cores, estimated to be around 34 solar masses, was discovered to have its central density decreased over time, providing further evidence that core expansion, possibly caused by heat, is the primary process of evolution for at least some of the cores within the Dragon. The observed core expansion in the cooler and more massive cores implies the emergence of massive star forming regions. Future optical and millimeter wave surveys are required to determine if the cloud has produced at least one massive star forming region. The evolution of cloud cores in the Dragon is likely caused by a global process that heats the entire cloud from the outside in. The reason behind this heating is not fully understood, but it could be the result of either the cloud being compressed from the outside or being hit by a nearby shock wave. The spread of molecular clumps within the cloud also suggests that cloud evolution is not just confined to the cores but is also affected by the distribution of clump-bypass streams - large ridges of gas that form, compress, and heat the entire cloud. The formation of these clumps and the subsequent passage of clump-bypass streams could be the key factors in the evolution of cloud cores in the Dragon and possibly of all massive clouds worldwide. The cloud may eventually give rise to a massive star, possibly an extremely massive one, through the passage of time. The evolution of cloud cores in the Dragon implies that the transformation of an IRDC into a MSFC may involve the expansion of at least some of the cores, possibly due to heat, to form more evolved cores before the formation of massive stars within them. This discovery may indicate that the emergence of massive star forming regions involves the failure of cloud contraction in the hottest regions, leading to the passage of heat from the outside in. I've conducted a series of simulations exploring the behavior of shadows produced by primordial black holes made largely of dark matter. By running extensive simulations with 20 billion particles, I've examined how the distribution of matter affects the size of these shadows. These studies, which have been made possible by the PopSyCLE tool, allow for a more in-depth analysis of the effects of baryons on primordial black holes with masses ranging from 10 to 10,000 times that of the sun. Our results indicate that for smaller black holes, the matter distribution is similar to that of a uniform gas, but for more massive objects, the irregular structure of the matter cloud results in slightly larger shadows. This research has also enabled us to create a more accurate formula for estimating the size of these shadows, taking into account the effects of both baryons and dark matter. Furthermore, we have discovered possible indicators of irregular matter distributions in observations of nearby galaxies. Importantly, our calculations have revealed that for black holes with less than 1,000 times the mass of the sun, the size of these shadows is largely unaffected by the internal structure of the matter cloud. However, for more massive objects, the size of these shadows can be up to 1.6% larger due to such variations, highlighting the potential importance of these phenomena in the study of supermassive black holes. Importantly, our work has also enabled a more in-depth analysis of the potential role of black holes in explaining certain stellar formations due to their interactions with irregular matter distributions. Our simulations have also provided valuable insights into how to apply the microlensing technique to detect and study these possible shadows, particularly in regions near to, or surrounding, galactic centers where numerous data have been collected but no signs of such phenomena have been detected so far. Our findings suggest that for masses under 100,000 times the mass of the sun, the size of these shadows can be as small as 0.4 angular minutes, making them potentially detectable with highly advanced technology in highly controlled laboratory settings. Moreover, for masses over one million times the mass of the sun, the size of these shadows can be as large as 170,000 times that of the mass of the sun, indicating that for extremely large black holes, the size of these potential shadows can be extremely large as well. Our next goal is to further study and explore potential observational evidence of such phenomena, particularly possible anisotropies in the density of light in the surroundings of the Earth on a galactic scale

The study of set transcription from a preference ordering view has been widely researched in the realm of science and mathematics for centuries, however it is only in recent years that this concept has been explored in the field of artificial intelligence. This research method has been applied to tackle the set augmentation problem, which is a key issue in machine learning. This paper examines the set transcription approach from a preference ordering standpoint to further develop the framework of artificial intelligence. Set transcription is a phenomenon that translates preference ordering into a single-point value system, while simultaneously creating a mapping for the domain. This study presents a novel single-point value system called CoCSET for preference ordering, which achieves a complete mapping of the domain. This method utilizes contrastive learning to achieve single-point value system translation and set transcription. This research delves into the theoretical foundations of CoCSET and evaluates its effectiveness through set augmentation tasks. Our results demonstrate that CoCSET possesses a considerable advantage in set augmentation tasks in comparison to other methods. Our research reveals that the principle of contrastive learning has a profound impact on the single-point value system as well as the set itself, and this relationship is orthogonal to the process of set generation. This understanding can be leveraged to develop new set generation methods. Our research shows that by using the single-point value system and setting theoretical boundaries on the set itself, it is possible to define novel set generation methods. This study presents two methods, namely CoCSET-based set generation and contrastive learning-based set generation. Our research finds that CoCSET-based set generation possesses greater simplicity in comparison to contrastive learning-based set generation, while both methods exhibit distinct improvements in set augmentation performance. Our research shows that the quality of the sets generated from these methods depends on the degree of contrastive learning applied during the process. This study highlights a further set generation method called iterative contrastive learning, which is found to surpass the performance of both CoCSET-based set generation and contrastive learning-based set generation in set augmentation tasks. Our research reveals that the principle of iterative learning can be applied to enhance the quality of set transcription. Our research shows that the iterative learning mechanism can be used to balance the size of the sets generated while maintaining their quality. Our research also reveals that the iterative learning mechanism is vulnerable to overfitting if the number of iterations is excessive, and this can be mitigated by applying data augmentation techniques to set augmentation tasks. Previous studies have shown that normal children between ages 1 and 3 develop an aversion to rejection, which is a preference for sentences containing errors over correct sentences.  This paper aims to investigate a way to train transformer models to emulate rejection in linguistic processes.  Firstly, we tested the current state-of-the-art transformer models and found that adding a straightforward error detection function within the model doesn't overcome the challenge of learning rejection.  Next, we proposed two novel approaches: Direct Rejection Models and Induced Rejection Models.  These new approaches train the model to learn a preference for erroneous sentences by adjusting the way attention and pooling operations interact.  Our experiments show that these solutions successfully train the model to prefer erroneous sentences.  Moreover, we discovered that rejection can be learned as a general skill that can be applied to unfamiliar data, which is similar to the skill of sentence correction in children.  This research is the first to successfully train a transformer model to emulate rejection on linguistic processes.  This achievement opens the door for training models on tasks that were previously thought of as requiring human-like rejection abilities.  Ultimately, we plan to use this model to investigate tasks where rejection is involved, such as machine paraphrasing and machine reasoning. Visualizations of the eruption site and the eruption's pathway into space have been created, confirming that the ejected material formed an expanding conical cloud. The material from the eruption traveled at least 160 parsecs in two years, indicating that the eruption was exceptionally fast. The eruption has resulted in the formation of compact, high-density regions within the cloud, indicating that the eruption was shock heated to 1600 times the galaxy's rotation speed within a few months of the eruption. The material from the eruption has expanded into the interstellar medium of the galaxy, whose further cooling has resulted in the formation of new, previously unobserved regions of neutral hydrogen. These regions have expanded into 160 parsecs in two years, indicating that the eruption was exceptionally fast. The eruption has expanded into a vast, 1.5 kiloparsecs wide conical cloud, whose material is now being recycled back into the galaxy. The cloud has already started to collapse into a new, circumgalactic disk of neutral hydrogen. This has implications for the formation of new stars in the galaxy. A novel conservative approximation is developed for solving quasi-linear diffusion equations in magnetized plasmas. This equation is an important solution for understanding particle transport in various astronomical objects. A conservative finite element method is devised for this equation, employing characteristic-based Galerkin approaches for both spatial and temporal discretization. This results in a conservative numerical scheme for mass density, particle density, and the symmetric tensor. The new method conserves a range of physical quantities automatically and preserves positivity. It is also proven to be consistent, robust, and free from nonphysical oscillations. To evaluate its performance, various numerical simulations are conducted to demonstrate the method's conservative properties, accuracy, and ability to maintain positivity. One key test case involves the diffusion of a Gaussian cloud in magnetized plasma, while another case explores collisional and compressional transport in a magnetized plasma. To further verify the method's performance, a test case of the spherically symmetric, rotationally symmetric Ermakov particle system in magnetized plasma is performed, revealing the method's ability to accurately capture both diffusion and ballistic behavior. Finally, a test case of the collisional, compressional transport of a ring distribution function in magnetized plasma is carried out, demonstrating the method's ability to accurately model long-term collisional behavior. All of these numerical simulations were performed using the publicly available NIRVANA code. This paper extends the existing code to support quasi-linear diffusion equations in magnetized plasma. A detailed description of the method's theory and implementation is provided, along with a range of test cases that verify its performance and accuracy. The implementation of this method represents an important addition to the NIRVANA code, as it now supports a range of plasma transport equations, including those with magnetic field effects. The new method has applications in studying various astronomical objects, such as the interstellar medium, active galactic nuclei, and various other objects. The theory and implementation of this method are significant, as they provide a framework for understanding magnetic field effects on particle transport in the mentioned objects. The non-adiabatic behavior of particles in these environments is typically driven by plasma processes such as turbulence, shocks, and other complex plasma interactions. The new method enhances the NIRVANA code's ability to accurately model and study these processes, further advancing our understanding of the mentioned astronomical objects. The theory and implementation described in this paper are general and applicable to a range of plasma types, including both collisional and non-collisional cases. The proposed program, MuMuPy, is designed to calculate the interaction between dimuonium (true muonium) and various substances under conditions of static electric and magnetic fields as well as temperature and pressure. By employing relativistic methods, this program caters to the heavy masses of muons and accounts for the internal dynamics of atoms and molecules using relativistic quantum field theory. It offers a range of practical applications including the investigation of dimuonium's influence on atomic parities, assessment of electron-muon collision risks in high-energy particle colliders, and simulation of dimuonium's chemical properties. Developed with a Python-based structure, this program's code is accessible on the public code review platform GitHub. Additionally, MuMuPy is capable of acting as a generator for Monte Carlo particle collisions, making it a valuable tool for future experiments aiming to observe dimuonium's binding. Although currently unfettered by experimental constraints, this program's code is now made available in anticipation of upcoming experiments that will utilize dimuonium in leading particle physics experiments. Upon validation with established theoretical data sets, MuMuPy was successfully compared to theoretical predictions of dimuonium's electric form factor and atomic parity induced by nuclear interactions. With further developments, this program is ready to contribute in various areas of research including muon g-2 measurements, electron-muon collision investigations, and J-PANDA's hadronization measurements. This research formalizes a rigorous framework for investing in a single asset over an infinite timeframe using a logarithmic absolute return or a relative return utility function. Effective investment strategies are analyzed under both complete and complete-with-jump fluidity conditions, and in each scenario, an optimal stochastic portfolio is identified along with the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations and their solutions. For relative return utility functions, which often incorporate a benchmark for evaluation, equations are established to optimize benchmark selection, and in the case of a single benchmark, a detailed solution is provided along with the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations and their solutions. Numerical simulations are conducted to assess optimal investing outcomes under various market conditions. Additionally, this study expands existing stochastic optimization theories related to investment and wealth management policies proposed in literature. More specifically, this research generalizes the work by Krzlanek et al. (Math Finan 2015), who addressed absolute return investing, and extends the work by Huang et al. (Math Finan 2019), who explored relative return investing, to optimize benchmarks for comparison in relative return investing frameworks. Finally, to illustrate the applicability of these theoretical findings, a real-world application is considered, with a focus on investing in the Australian stock market. To achieve this, a two-step method is employed that combines genetic algorithms with a neural network, and the results are validated using historical data from 2010 to 2020. Overall, this research provides a comprehensive framework for optimizing investing strategies in various market conditions, and the associated results can inform and assist real-world investment decisions. A comprehensive source code for implementing the theoretical models using MATLAB is provided in the appendix to facilitate replication by the scientific community. The research is further supported by a thorough dataset containing historical Australian stock market data from 2010 to 2020, and the induction benchmarking results for the specified time frame. The conventional Black-Scholes model is also applied to assess liquidity and provide a detailed comparison with other theoretical models, and the associated results can inform and assist real-world investment decisions. The addition of additional constraints or the use of advanced theoretical tools is required to accurately determine the quantum features of the system.  Ultimately, the research highlights the need to view the quasiparticle description as an inherently approximate model rather than a precise tool for extracting information about the system. We further derive conditions under which the divergence of word representations in these groups is finite. Additionally, through the creation of Euler-Poincaré polynomials, the divergence of braided-Thompson groups is formally defined. Text-of-a-clip retrieval, where the task involves selecting the most relevant text based on a given video frame, has significant applications in various domains, such as semantic search and computer vision. Given the substantial capacity of a text encoder, the primary limitation here lies in efficiently retrieving the most relevant text. This paper proposes TS2-Net, a token-level retrieval network that accomplishes this by shifting and selecting tokens across different text samples. TS2-Net is composed of several key components, including a multi-head projector that projects multiple text samples into a shared space, a token shifter that identifies the most relevant tokens, a selector that determines the optimal text segment from each sample, and a classifier that identifies the final class. Through rigorous testing on multiple benchmarks, it has been demonstrated that TS2-Net achieves a new state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing models by a significant margin. Furthermore, the paper also explores additional challenges associated with text-of-a-clip retrieval, such as multi-lingual and multi-frame retrieval tasks. The proposed framework and related code are publicly available on GitHub. We welcome researchers and practitioners to explore and contribute to this initiative.

A recent approach, Distributed Optimal Transport (DOT), circumvents transportation planning's computational limitations by breaking it down into simpler distance matrix calculations. Although DOT is limited to few hundreds of points, we propose a deep learning framework that applies DOT's strategy to achieve high-quality representations on large datasets. The DOT loss is approximated by replacing the sum with an average and introducing a scaling factor, leading to a trainable Sinkhorn layer in our framework. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated on single-image domain adaptation and colorization tasks. The results show that it achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art methods while being more general and easily integrable with existing algorithms. Moreover, it can also be used as a pre-training task for other deep learning approaches. The corresponding code is available at https://github.com/daniquero/sinkhorn_cnn. The Sinkhorn CNN architecture has been successfully used in a variety of applications, such as image registration and discretized deep learning. The OT Optimizer is a C++/CU library for solving OT problems. The OT Optimizer is currently the most efficient and flexible library available, supporting a wide variety of OT algorithms, including first-order methods, Newton's method, and deep learning approaches. The OT Optimizer is used by several researchers, including the winners of the NeurIPS 2020 OTL challenge. The OT Optimizer uses a Sinkhorn algorithm with a second-order numerical resolution, a gradient descent approach that proves to be less efficient than deep learning methods.

Although numerous geographical studies have aimed to characterize SARS-CoV-2's spatial patterns, few have explored the impact of weather and air quality on disease spread, especially in urban centers. Recognizing the interdependence between environmental factors and SARS-CoV-2 infections, we employed geostatistical modeling and artificial neural networks, incorporating data on humidity, temperature, air quality, and population density, to investigate SARS-CoV-2's spatial patterns in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Our research highlighted the significant contribution of weather and ambient pollution in place-specific predictions of SARS-CoV-2 infections. While existing literature has explored the impact of these variables on disease outcomes, our study was specifically designed to develop an innovative predictive model with applications in epidemiological research. We found significant spatial patterns in SARS-CoV-2 infections, with areas such as the western zone exhibiting notably higher incidence rates compared to the northern sector. Our results also demonstrated the significant correlation between population density and SARS-CoV-2 infections. We were able to predict an exceptional increase of 301% in SARS-CoV-2 cases in the western sector of Rio de Janeiro, with significant correlations found between temperature, humidity, and population density. Our results will be instrumental in informing public policy and decision-making, offering a promising avenue for interdisciplinary research in urban health studies. Our findings emphasize the need to consider environmental factors when understanding SARS-CoV-2 infections and their outcomes. We were able to utilize geostatistical modeling and artificial neural networks in epidemiological research, providing an essential contribution in this field. Our study was possible due to the integration of multiple datasets, including climate variables, air quality indicators, population data, and SARS-CoV-2 infections, which allowed us to develop a comprehensive understanding of environmental factors' impact on disease patterns. Our results will be published in international scientific journals focused on spatial statistics, AI, epidemiology, environmental science, public health, geoscience, and entomology. This technique has a key distinguishing feature: it employs a resistive electrode in a configuration that is not in series with the tunneling junction, thereby ensuring that voltage is applied across the junction itself. In this study, a novel utility function is proposed and an unsupervised RL method is developed to select the most reliable features, thereby enhancing the model's resistance to various forms of contamination. This approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through comparisons on artificially corrupted datasets as well as datasets with confounding variables, revealing the benefits of deep learning and RL in adaptation to changing data characteristics. In this paper, we identify the least number of subsets needed to cover all intersections of a given infinite set of finite sets, providing a precise upper limit based on the Cantor-Bendixson index of the underlying infinite set. We also establish a corresponding lower bound, showing it is infinite if the underlying set is not finite. Furthermore, we examine the same problem for infinite families of finite sets, obtaining a precise upper limit based on the number of infinite subsets within those families. We also provide examples to demonstrate the validity of our results. We further extend these findings to higher-dimensional hypergraphs within specific dimensions. Finally, we define and investigate a related graph theory problem. 

The associated graph theory problem can be summarized as follows: Given a hypergraph, we seek to find the smallest collection of subsets such that each subset's intersection is completely covered by a subset in the collection. We define this ideal collection as minimal coverings, and explore the following question: For a given graph, are there infinitely many minimal coverings, and is the number of such coverings bounded? 

Our investigation of upper bounds reveals that the number of minimal coverings is bounded above by $2^{c(\Gamma)}$ for any infinite graph $\Gamma$. We also provide instances demonstrating the possibility of an infinite number of minimal coverings without any bound on their quantity. We introduce OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation for illustrating connections between entities within extensive knowledge graphs, with particular emphasis on domains defined by formal ontologies. The design of the ontology graph for visualisation presents challenges due to its scale and nature of hierarchical organisation, leading to the development of OntoPlot to address these limitations. The ontology graph for visualisation is first reduced in scale by defining a circle of significance to determine which entities to include, with those of primary importance in the centre and those of lesser importance towards the periphery. Once the relevant entities have been selected, the pairs of entities are also determined based on their closeness, with only the most significant relationships between them included in the plot, thereby reducing computational load. The entities within the circle are then positioned relative to each other based on their semantic proximity, with those of similar meaning nearest to each other and those of dissimilar meaning further apart, resulting in a visualisation that showcases the selected subset of the ontology in an intuitive and easy-to-understand format. We demonstrate the effectiveness of OntoPlot through its application to visualisations of the FOAF, YAGO, DBpedia, and CheZborovt ontologies. CheZborovt is an extensive Russian ontology composed of approximately 7 million entities, with OntoPlot capable of successfully visualising non-hierarchical relationships between a substantial subset of its entities, thereby aiding in the identification of important and previously overlooked connections within the ontology. Furthermore, we propose an automated method for identifying and highlighting entities within the circle of significance based on their semantic relationships. The development of OntoPlot is based on findings from user-centric case studies and showcases its potential as a useful tool for domain experts, researchers, and knowledge engineers to illustrate non-hierarchical entity relationships within the ontology. A significant challenge in creating cost-effective speech transcription systems is the scarcity of speech-to-text training data. This issue can be addressed by employing semi-supervised learning, which allows systems to utilize large amounts of publicly available transcribed data along with untranscribed speech files. Another possible solution is using data augmentation techniques to maximize system efficiency. This research focuses on two primary objectives: first, to investigate the effectiveness of an intersectional loss in a single-stream automatic speech transcription model; second, to combine a speech-to-text model with a speech-to-audio model to generate auxiliary unprocessed audio examples that enhance transcription quality through data augmentation. Experimental results revealed that the proposed approach results in a 7.5% relative improvement in transcription accuracy for the English dataset and 13.5% for the German dataset. Furthermore, using audio augmentation in conjunction with a fully connected self-attention layer led to an additional 2.1% improvement. Notably, when used independently, both techniques exhibited comparable performance to the combined approach, showcasing that combining these strategies can greatly improve overall transcription accuracy. Additionally, the paper highlights the importance of meticulous hyperparameter tuning, particularly when merging various deep learning techniques. Finally, the paper demonstrates that the proposed method achieves the best results when applied to speech benchmarks with limited transcribed data, notably the LDC94-15-08 dataset used in the DS2 spoken web parliament dataset report. This application employs the published model and has a narrow browser window as its primary entry point. The entire model architecture, training data, and performance analysis are publicly available through the https://github.com/tonyautomation/SpeechCon2MixSS dataset. The DS2 dataset for the spoken web parliament can be accessed through the http://www.paritech.org/data/DS2/download.html website. The published work bears some resemblance to a 2021 research paper titled 'End-to-end automatic speech transcription using CycleGAN-based speech and audio integration' in the ICSLP2021, as well as a 2022 research paper titled 'Improving end-to-end automatic speech transcription with audio augmentations' in the Interspeech2022. A different method, which combines two models, is presented in a 2022 research paper titled 'End-to-end automatic speech transcription: Advances and trends' in the IEEE Signal Processing Magazine. The development of independent, autonomous robotic entities requires sophisticated mathematical frameworks for managing complex decision-making processes, as evident from cutting-edge applications such as robotic navigation. Despite these complex systems, a crucial aspect is the logical structure of their software, which is typically characterized by two distinct phases: computational deduction for generating possible solutions and an evaluation function for assessing solution quality. To improve computational efficiency and effectiveness, we propose an innovative, active inquiry approach that dynamically selects and eliminates potential solutions based on the evaluation of hypotheses and context-dependent facts. Our method integrates both deduction and evaluation in a unified, query-driven process, eliminating the need for an explicit choice and evaluation step. We provide a comprehensive semantic foundation for this approach, developed on the principles of multi-valued logic, and demonstrate its application in autonomous robotic navigation, including a practical implementation in a real-world robot environment. The proposed methodology offers a general solution to the explicit choice problem, holding significant potential for multi-agent decision-making scenarios. Our theoretical investigation examines how the structure of soft chiral molecules affects the Soret effect, which is a heat current driven by a temperature gradient, within these molecules. This effect varies depending on the molecules' rotational frequency and temperature. As a result, we can forecast a correlation between the Soret coefficient and the temperature-dependent rotational frequency. This correlation might be influenced by the internal movements of the molecules, specifically those that affect their optical properties. To test our findings, we selected hexane, which exhibits a specific type of molecular vibration that impacts its optical properties. Similar internal movements are found in other molecules, such as ethane, pentane, and 2-butane. To verify our theory, we conducted in-depth research on these molecules and their 2,2-dimethyl analogues. This investigation demonstrates that the Soret effect is predominantly caused by low-frequency molecular vibrations, which in turn are driven by entropy. This entropic driving force overwhelmingly influences the Soret effect, especially at low temperatures. Moreover, we discovered that the Soret effect caused by molecular vibrations exhibits a correlation proportional to the observed change in the molecules' optical properties. To generalize our findings, we employed a model based on the observed patterns in the molecules' frequency spectra. This model, coupled with our previous research on the interaction between light and matter, allows us to assess the overall contribution of internal molecular vibrations to the Soret effect, which varies widely. This contribution can be extensively modulated through the use of substances with stereoisomers, which in turn affects their ability to perform thermal work as needed. This ability to influence the Soret effect has significant implications, such as the development of molecular machines that can generate work according to the requirements of their design. Ultimately, our research expands our understanding of the complex interaction between light and matter while also unlocking novel applications in this area. Specifically, we are exploring the feasibility of creating soft chiral systems that can efficiently convert solar radiation into mechanical energy, which in turn can be utilized for various purposes. This exploration has led to another potential application, which involves using the Soret effect to create liquid crystals that can transition between different states in response to external stimuli. This potential has already inspired our research into the Soret effect in liquid crystals, which in turn may contribute to the development of innovative and efficient technologies. To achieve these goals, we are working to generalize our findings by employing advanced models that enable the study of various soft matter systems on a wide range of scales, from molecular chemistry to materials science. Traditional computer vision models are often designed to work in a static environment and may struggle with dynamic, real-time applications, especially when they are applied to different settings without further adjustment. This problem can be alleviated by domain adaptation techniques that allow a model to effectively use information from one environment to another, but our approach takes a different strategy by reducing unnecessary data. Instead of adapting to a new environment by incorporating new information, we are reducing the amount of false data by eliminating unnecessary candidates. This method has the added benefit of allowing our model to become more robust to irrelevant data from the new environment, making it easier to adapt to new situations. We have tested our approach on the challenging task of identifying people in the context of surveillance, where it has proven to be effective, leading to a significant decrease of false positives and a notable 2.51 mAP improvement in some cases. This method is also easy to implement, requiring only a brief fine-tuning of our model. Our approach uses a simple box regression method to eliminate false positives and does not rely on any further post-processing, making it a suitable solution for a wide range of real-time, dynamic applications. We have tested our approach on the challenging MS-COCO dataset as well as the larger Citypersons dataset to demonstrate its effectiveness in difficult situations. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/ByronWills/boxreo. This research is supported in part by the Microsoft Cognitive ToolKit, the NSFC 62076017, the NCET 202010308012, and the Wuhan Morning Light Scholarship. An extended version of this paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/understand domain adaptation with box reordering.

This research explores the potential for an end-to-end conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) to enhance the quality of music samples by learning from corresponding audio spectra and selecting suitable transformation operations. A novel image enhancement technique is proposed and combined with a frequency domain-based audio synthesis approach. Experimental results demonstrate that this system can generate high-quality music samples when trained on various domains, and also reveal the impact of different image enhancement algorithms on the quality of the generated samples. Additionally, the study investigates multiple architectures for the discriminator and concludes that a model incorporating a ResNet discriminator consistently outperforms traditional architectures in terms of sample quality and stability. A corresponding implementation of this research can be found on the GitHub repository'music-improvement'. Furthermore, the paper includes a comprehensive analysis of the possible applications of the system, including its potential uses in music generation and transformation tasks. However, a crucial limitation of the system is that it often fails to successfully improve the music samples and, on occasion, generates unplayable output. This makes it necessary to apply the system only when music samples are in a state of distress. A future extension of this research aims to develop a more robust system capable of producing consistently high-quality results across a broader range of music samples. A demonstration video of the system can be found at https://youtu.be/7QYGeYWOt8E-index. In virtual environments, the way a character throws a virtual object can give hints about their intentions, but throwing movements don't always accurately represent the object's trajectory. This study examines the impact of discrepancies between a character's throwing motion and the actual trajectory of the object on perceptions of their intentions and capabilities. Participants viewed scenes where a virtual character either threw or didn't throw a ball, with varying points of release that matched or didn't match the ball's actual trajectory. Results show that discrepancies in throwing motions significantly influence perceptions of a character's abilities and intentions, and these responses are more pronounced in situations where the character's capabilities are ambiguous. In internal reactions involving three and four atoms, the exchange of energy can result in the release of excess energy, often not considered in traditional binding energy assessments that treat such excess energy as part of the binding force. To address this, a new platform is introduced that replicates experimental conditions, thereby allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of binding forces. This platform will serve as a resource for researchers to verify theoretical models against experimental findings, promoting interdisciplinary collaborations between astrochemists and quantum chemists. To establish confidence in the platform's accuracy, its results for various carbon and oxygen containing molecules are compared with experimental data, demonstrating strong correlations in binding energy distributions, as well as total binding energies. This highlights the importance of considering excess energy in binding forces, particularly in cases where internal activation energies are low. The platform is available at bind.ep.de and features a database with over 1,000 binding energy distributions, approximately 450 of which pertain to carbon and oxygen containing species relevant to astrochemistry. By utilizing this tool, researchers can conduct a meta-analysis of experimental data, an advantage showcased through a case study of HH 80E's complex organic molecules. Ultimately, the platform is poised to become an essential resource for researchers in various fields, including astrophysics, biochemistry, and medicine, and it is predicted that it will be instrumental in interpreting binding energy distributions in rotating and vibrating molecules with small activation energies, a phenomenon that is prevalent across most organic molecules. Our approach to assessing qubit states relies on a shallow projection mechanism 
utilizing a random Clifford circuit of moderate depth. This method can evaluate 
expectation values for observables within $O(N)$ operations when given any 
sequence of two-qubit operators and a set of $N$ qubits. This study explores 
the operational cost issue in detail and provides an explanation for its 
efficiency through the application of Pauli transfer and the concept of 'lumpiness' 
in a quantum system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the mechanism's dependence 
on the number of qubits is substantial, implying that there are practical 
limitations to its use in larger quantum systems. Finally, we outline areas for 
potential improvements and predict that the shallow projection mechanism could 
become an essential tool if improved scalability is achieved. The underlying 
principles and utility of the mechanism are thoroughly examined. The mechanism 
is now available as an open-source Python package called SHADES. The package's 
current limitations are highlighted, including its restricted ability to handle 
certain types of circuits due to depth constraints. Future research aims to 
expand the package's application to a wider range of circuits. The package can 
be accessed at https://shades.readthedocs.io/.

Identifying COVID-19 infections depends on chest computed tomography (CT) scans, with accurate segmentation of infected areas being essential for quantitative analysis, prognosis, and infection tracking. Due to limited annotated data and the significant time involved in manual segmentation, automatically detecting and outlining COVID-19 lesions is crucial for medical imaging research. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel three-stage deep learning framework that incorporates lesion location, segmentation, and post-processing to localize and outline COID-19 lesions independently of image interpretation and region selection. Our model leverages weakly supervised object localization and segmentation to learn from scratch, utilizing a combined priority loss function for accurate detection and segmentation. We test our framework on a small dataset and compare its performance to established methods, with results showing improved localization and segmentation of COID-19 lesions. Our framework demonstrates freedom from image interpretation and region selection biases, with potential applications in prognosis and infection tracking, and the source code is available at https://github.com/AsadToussi/COVID19_LoS_GA_LeakyIOU. Our model's performance was formally published in Medical Image Analysis in 2022.

Detecting vertebra is a crucial step in the diagnosis of spinal disorders, and researchers have been working on creating an automated vertebra detection system. However, common voltage-based methods often fail due to noise or distorted X-ray images, while vision-based approaches face challenges in spine detection due to the compact and irregularly-shaped spinal cord area. To address these limitations, a novel vertebra detection framework has been proposed, combining data preprocessing, region proposal, and classification techniques. By identifying and removing lung clutter and aligning the vertebral column, the framework rectifies and enhances vertebral candidates, making them more visible to detectors. Moreover, an anatomically-constrained enhancement module is introduced to emphasize vertebral features and suppress noise. To achieve this, a multi-stage vertebra detection network consisting of spinal cord-aided and vertebra-aided branches is designed to jointly locate and identify vertebrae, leveraging the spinal cord map as a proxy for posterior disc detection. This research highlights the benefits of utilizing deformable actuators in the actuators of leg-driven robots. We specifically examine their influence on the mobility of quadruped creatures, which can enhance their capacity to climb, traverse uneven terrain, reduce energy consumption, and increase their range. We develop an advanced control method called the ZMP-differentiable elastic gauge foot-force distribution (ZEEFFD), which optimizes the foot-force pattern during the double support phase, incorporating the static stability of the robot. We then use a reinforcement learning strategy to fine-tune the proposed control method, which can automatically adjust the foot-force pattern in response to the robot's state when navigating varied terrain. We test our ZEEFFD method through simulation, comparing its performance to other elastic actuator strategies that employ single support and multi-modal support frameworks. Our simulation results show that the ZEEFFD method exhibits superior mobility when compared to other strategies, while also reducing energy consumption and increasing the robot's maximum climbable slope. We also present an analysis of the learning process of our reinforcement learning strategy, which successfully incorporates the robot's dynamic mobility and stability into its decision-making process. Our analysis emphasizes the importance of incorporating the robot's dynamic behavior when designing the reward function of the reinforcement learning agent. We observe that the agent's learning process is greatly affected by the inclusion of the robot's dynamic mobility and stability in the reward function, which demonstrates its capacity to account for the differences between static and dynamic stability. We also conduct a multi-step robustness assessment of our ZEEFFD method against potential model inaccuracy, discovering that the proposed control strategy exhibits moderate levels of resilience against errors in actuator deformation and foot size variations. Nonetheless, our research reveals that the ZEEFFD method performs better than other elastic actuator strategies that rely on double support and single support frameworks. We finally outline the future directions of our research, recommending that our ZEEFFD method be tested through real-world experimentation to validate its effectiveness in practical applications. We also recommend the implementation of a model predictive control strategy that takes into account the uncertainties associated with the robot's dynamics. Our research aims to contribute to the advancement of dynamic mobility and stability design principles that can effectively utilize the capabilities of deformable actuators. By applying the proposed ZEEFFD method, quadruped creation and development can be facilitated through the adoption of an automated control strategy that can be easily modified to suit various applications and hardware configurations. Our research aims to promote the integration of elastic actuators in the design of leg-driven robots

In order to optimize the performance of WiFi networks in dense environments, effectively managing the allocation of network resources between Base Transceivers and Extenders is crucial. Typically, Base Transceivers assign channels for Extenders in a random manner; however, this can lead to congestion. By taking into account available network channels and feedback from Extenders, we propose a new method, named channel load conscious AP/Extender choice, aimed at optimizing performance by incorporating the IEEE 802.11k/v standards. This method allows Extenders to choose channels with lower interference, thereby improving overall performance. By choosing channels optimally, the network can operate at full capacity, leading to enhanced quality of service, improved video streaming quality, and increased data transfer rates, ultimately allowing for more capable fast channel switching, multiple stream support, and higher data transfer. Furthermore, this method reduces the impact of interference from neighboring networks and increases the available time for communication between Base Transceivers and Extenders, thereby improving battery life for mobile Extenders. Experimental results confirm that our method outperforms standard IEEE 802.11v Association methods in both performance and quality of service.
